Molecular methods are also available (see section 7.4). Source and occurrence EHEC has been detected in a variety of water and wastewater environments includ- ing surface water and drinking-water sourced from vulnerable groundwater supplies, with most studies focusing on E. coli O157. Prevalence is influenced primarily by the presence of animal faecal material, particularly from cattle. The presence of human faecal waste including sewage (untreated or partially treated) may also be a contribut- ing factor. Persistence in water is considered to be moderate (up to 1 month at 20 °C), with survival influenced by environmental conditions. Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4), control measures to manage potential risks from EHEC should include protection of source waters from contamination by human and animal faecal wastes (including extra vigilance during heavy rain), application of adequate water treatment processes, and protection of drinking-water quality during storage and distribution. Chlorine and UV light are effective drinking-water disinfectants against EHEC. Non-pathogenic E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is a suitable in- dicator for the possible presence or absence of EHEC in drinking-water (see section 11.6). This applies even though standard tests for E. coli based on β-glucuronidase activity will not detect EHEC. Bibliography WHO (2025) Enterohaemorrhagic Escherichia coli. Background document for the WHO Guidelines for drinking-water quality and the WHO Guidelines on sanitation and health. Geneva, World Health Organization. Francisella tularensis Significance in drinking‑water There is strong evidence for waterborne transmission of Francisella tularensis from multiple outbreaks associated with drinking-water sources that were contaminated from animal carcasses and excreta with no or inadequate treatment. General description Francisella are Gram-negative, non-spore-forming, coccobacilli. There are at least 10 species of Francisella, but F. tularensis is the only species of concern for waterborne transmission. F. tularensis is further subdivided into four subspecies: F. tularensis subsp. tularensis (type A), F. tularensis subsp. holarctica (type B), F. tularensis subsp. mediasiatica and F. tularensis subsp. novicida. Subspecies type A is the most virulent and is predominantly found in North America; subspecies type B is less virulent, is widely distributed in the northern hemisphere and is the subspecies commonly linked to waterborne outbreaks. Human health effects Infection with F. tularensis can be asymptomatic or cause tularaemia, which is char - acterized by sudden onset of high fever, chills, general malaise, headache, anorexia

262 263 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA and fatigue. The clinical outcomes depend on the route of transmission. The oropha- ryngeal form is most commonly associated with waterborne transmission, although oculoglandular, ulceroglandular and pneumonic forms have been reported. Inhalation of F. tularensis in aerosols from dust and hay can result in acute and life-threatening pneumonia. A typhoidal form, probably associated with inhalation of contaminated aerosols, causes high fever and confusion, and mimics typhoid. Symptoms of oropha- ryngeal infections include a sore throat/tonsillitis, mouth ulcers, pharyngitis, swollen cervical lymph nodes with possible discharge of pus and occasionally gastrointestinal symptoms including diarrhoea. Treatment with antibiotics may be recommended for severe cases of tularaemia. Development of antibiotic resistance has not been identi- fied, but is a concern. Epidemiology Tularaemia is generally restricted to the northern hemisphere, with isolated cases in Australia. The reported annual rates of disease are 0.1–0.3/100 000 people (based on an analysis published in 2021), while in the United States of America, the annual rate is <0.1/100 000 people (based on an analysis published in 2023). Generally, tularae- mia is more common in males with prevalence highest between 45 and 64 years of age. However, for waterborne tularaemia, children and adults, as well as males and females, are equally affected. Endemic disease occurs primarily during warm weather and is primarily related to insect bites. In contrast, during colder seasons, infections usually occur through contaminated drinking-water consumption. Transmission There are multiple modes of transmission of F. tularensis to humans, including: direct contact with infected rodents, their carcasses or their excreta; bites from ticks, fleas and mosquitoes; consumption of contaminated food or water; contact with contami- nated water or soils; and inhalation of aerosols from dust or hay. There is no evidence of person-to-person transmission. The relative infectivity of F. tularensis can vary depending on the subspecies, the mode of transmission and the form of disease. Infectivity from oral exposure is low, with estimated doses of 10 6–108 organisms. The incubation period is typically 3–5 days. Detection methods Culture-based methods are available for F. tularensis, although isolation can be chal- lenging because it is fastidious and slow growing. Molecular and immunological methods are also available (see section 7.4). Source and occurrence There are limited data on the occurrence of Francisella , but it has been detected in surface water and inadequately treated drinking-water with prevalence influenced by contamination by animal carcasses and faecal material, particularly rodents. F. tular - ensis can survive for at least moderate periods in water (1 week to 1 month at 20 °C). However, longer persistence can be supported by interactions with amoebae and in biofilms.

264 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4 ), control measures to manage potential risks from F. tularensis should include protection of source waters from access by rodents and con- tamination by animal carcasses or excreta, application of adequate water treatment processes, and protection of drinking-water quality from external contamination during storage and distribution. Control strategies to reduce biofilm formation can also reduce the potential for F. tularensis to survive in distribution systems. F. tular - ensis is moderately resistant to chlorine doses used in drinking-water treatment, but it can be effective provided adequate contact times are applied. UV light is an effective drinking-water disinfectant against F . tularensis. Due to longer survival of F. tular - ensis in water, E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator for its possible presence or absence in drinking-water (see section 11.6). Bibliography WHO (2025) Francisella tularensis. Background document for the WHO Guidelines for drinking- water quality. Geneva, World Health Organization. Helicobacter pylori Significance in drinking‑water There is moderate evidence for Helicobacter pylori as a cause of waterborne disease. The presence of H. pylori in drinking-water and epidemiological evidence indicating higher rates of infection associated with drinking untreated water, as well as inadequate sanitation and hygiene, provide evidence of waterborne transmission, particularly in low-income countries. General description H. pylori is a Gram-negative, spiral-shaped, motile bacterium. There are over 40 spe- cies of Helicobacter, but only H. pylori has been identified as a major human pathogen. Human health effects Although most H. pylori infections are asymptomatic, the bacteria can cause acute and chronic gastritis. H. pylori is a significant risk factor for peptic ulcer disease, mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma and gastric cancer in adults, and is epidemiologically associated with gastric cancer. The majority of H. pylori infections are initiated in childhood, and, without treatment, can be lifelong. Increasing rates of resistance of H. pylori to front-line antibiotics and declining rates of antimicrobial eradication have been reported. Epidemiology H. pylori is prevalent throughout the world. Most infections are acquired during child- hood, but symptoms generally do not appear until adulthood. It has been estimated (in a review published in 2017) that about one in three adults in high-income coun- tries are infected, while adults from low- and middle-income countries have higher prevalence ranging from 50% to 80%. A similar pattern of prevalence in children has been estimated. Gender does not seem to affect the risk of infection. Prevalence has

264 265 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA been decreasing over time, particularly in high-income countries. High incidence in indigenous communities has been reported globally. Transmission H. pylori is likely transmitted by ingestion of organisms in vomit and gastric juices through the oral and gastro–oral pathways. This is supported by the detection of high quantities of H. pylori in these fluids. Faecal–oral transmission is also considered pos- sible, although few studies have successfully isolated the pathogen in faeces. Direct person-to-person contact within families has been identified as the most likely route of transmission, because the infection tends to cluster within households. Lower eco- nomic status, more siblings, crowding, infected mothers and not having access to sew- age systems have been associated with higher H. pylori prevalence. Additional risk factors include drinking untreated water and eating in unhygienic conditions. Other transmission sources include contaminated food, and working in soil or water-related jobs or in health care. Primates, domestic cats, sheep and houseflies have also been identified as potential hosts, but zoonotic transmission has not been demonstrated. The infectivity and incubation period are uncertain, but in a human volunteer study, inocula of 10 4–1010 organisms caused illness that occurred sporadically af- ter 3 days and peaked between 9 and 12 days. Infection does not appear to lead to immunity. Detection methods Culture and molecular methods for H. pylori are available (see section 7.4). Culture methods are challenging as H. pylori is fastidious, microaerophilic and slow growing. Amoeba co-culture has been shown to enhance the growth of H. pylori before applica- tion of culture methods. Source and occurrence There are limited data on the occurrence of H. pylori in water and wastewater environ- ments due to the challenges in detecting these organisms in environmental samples. However, they have been detected in surface water, groundwater and inadequately treated drinking-water, with prevalence influenced by the presence of sewage (un- treated or partially treated). The persistence of H. pylori in surface water, based on culturability, is short (up to 1 week at 20 °C), but biofilms and free-living amoebae may increase the persistence of H. pylori. Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4 ), control measures to manage potential risks from H. pylori should include protection of source waters from contamination by faecal wastes, application of adequate water treatment processes and protection of drinking-water quality during storage and distribution. Control strategies to reduce biofilm formation can also reduce the potential for H. pylori to survive in distribution systems. Chlorine and UV light are effective disinfectants against H. pylori. As there is some evidence of the occurrence of H. pylori in faeces, E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) may be a suitable indicator of its possible presence in drinking-water, but since H. pylori may

266 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA persist in biofilms in drinking-water systems, the absence of E. coli is not a suitable indicator for its absence (see section 11.6). Bibliography WHO (2025) Helicobacter pylori. Background document for the WHO Guidelines for drinking- water quality and the WHO Guidelines on sanitation and health. Geneva, World Health Organization. Klebsiella Significance in drinking‑water Klebsiella are of low health significance in drinking-water. Although Klebsiella can colonize drinking-water distribution systems, there is no evidence linking transmis- sion with drinking-water for the general population. However, transmission of non- gastrointestinal infections by Klebsiella to susceptible patients in health-care settings may be possible. General description Klebsiella are Gram-negative, non-motile, rod-shaped bacteria. The genus consists of several species; many of these are natural members of the microbiome of most humans and many other animal hosts. However, K. pneumoniae and K. oxytoca are of poten- tial concern to human health. Human health effects Klebsiella especially K. pneumoniae and K. oxytoca, are opportunistic pathogens that cause nosocomial infection, illness and death. They are major causes of pneumo- nia, infections of the urinary and gastrointestinal tracts, and infections associated with in-dwelling catheters, burns, wounds and surgery, as well as liver abscesses and septicaemia. Epidemiology Klebsiella are one of the most important causes of death due to bacterial infections including those associated with antimicrobial resistance. Patients with impaired im- mune systems, such as elderly people or very young children, and those with excessive burns, wounds, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)/acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) infection, respiratory deficiencies, diabetes, malignancies or under- going immunosuppressive therapy are at the highest risk of infection. Transmission In health-care facilities, person-to-person contact or contact with contaminated fomi- tes are the most common transmission routes. In particular, transmission of K. pneu- moniae and K. oxytoca in health-care settings is associated with frequent contact with patients (e.g. in intensive care units). Factors that increase the likelihood of nosocomial infections include the presence of invasive devices such as respiratory support equip- ment and urinary catheters, post-surgical sites and wounds, and the use of antibiotics. Contaminated water, including biofilms and aerosols, are suspected sources of expo-

266 267 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA sure in health-care facilities, but this link is not confirmed. Sinks contaminated with K. pneumoniae and K. oxytoca have been implicated in hospital outbreaks of illness. The infectivity of K. pneumoniae or other species through drinking-water is un- known. No human infectivity dose–response studies have been conducted for any of the plausible exposure routes, such as water or air. However, based on animal studies, the relative infectivity is probably low. Detection methods Klebsiella can be detected in drinking-water by standard culture-based methods for coliform and thermotolerant coliform bacteria. However, this must be followed by bio- chemical methods to distinguish them from the other bacteria in this group. Molecular methods are also available (see section 7.4). Source and occurrence Klebsiella are common soil and water organisms. Klebsiella can grow in surface wa- ter receiving nutrient-rich industrial wastes (e.g. pulp and paper mills, textile plants, sugar cane processing plants). These species are typically not pathogenic. Klebsiella can also be detected in water environments impacted by faecal contamination, with Klebsiella commonly detected in the faeces of many healthy humans and animals. As a confounder, however, some species, that may not be faecal in origin, such as K. oxytoca can colonize drinking-water distribution systems and result in an indication of false-positive faecal contamination where thermotolerant coliform testing is used. Klebsiella can grow and persist for long periods in water (over 1 month at 20 °C). Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4), control measures that effectively manage the presence and growth of bacteria in drinking-water supplies will control Klebsiella . These in- clude protection of source waters from contamination by human and animal faecal wastes or industrial wastes (e.g. pulp and paper mills), application of adequate treat- ment processes and effective biofilm management in distribution systems and build- ing water systems including health-care facilities. WSPs for health-care facilities need to also consider the susceptibilities of patients. Chlorine is an effective drinking-water disinfectant against Klebsiella . As Klebsiella include environmental strains that can persist and grow in water, E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indica- tor for their possible presence or absence in drinking-water. Bibliography WHO (2025) Klebsiella. Background document for the WHO Guidelines for drinking-water quality. Geneva, World Health Organization. Legionella Significance in drinking‑water There is strong evidence for waterborne transmission of Legionella , with large num- bers of outbreaks associated with drinking-water systems including hot water systems and devices such as cooling towers and spas. Legionella can be the most significant waterborne pathogen in high-income countries.

268 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA General description Legionella are Gram-negative, rod-shaped, non-spore-forming, motile bacteria. They are found in a wide range of soil and water environments, primarily within free-living amoebae in biofilms, but also in sludges and sediments. Thirty of 61 species of Legionella have been associated with disease (legionel- losis). L. pneumophila, particularly serogroup 1, is the major waterborne pathogenic species, and is reported to cause most cases of legionellosis worldwide. A second spe- cies, L. longbeachae, associated with potting mixes and soils, causes about 5% of cases of legionellosis worldwide, but in Australia and New Zealand, it causes about 50% of cases. Other species associated with infrequent cases include L. anisa, L. bozemanii, L. feelii, L. gormanii and L. micdadei. Human health effects Legionella are opportunistic pathogens. Legionellosis can take one of two forms: Legionnaires’ disease or Pontiac fever. The former is a pneumonic illness with initial symptoms including fever, loss of appetite, headache, malaise, dry cough and lethargy; other symptoms can include muscle pain, nausea, diarrhoea and confusion. The most frequent complications of Legionnaires’ disease are respiratory failure, shock, and acute kidney and multi-organ failure. The death rate (including based on a review pub- lished in 2017) is generally within the range of 5% to more than 10%, with increased mortality in immunosuppressed and nosocomial cases. Pontiac fever is an acute but milder non-pneumonic and self-limiting disease with symptoms similar to those of influenza including fever, headache, nausea, vomiting, aching muscles, joint pain and coughing. Asymptomatic infections are common. Antibiotic resistance is rare. Epidemiology The worldwide incidence of legionellosis is unknown because of limitations in surveil- lance. Most reported data are from high-income countries, with national annual inci- dence rates ranging from 0.1 to 77 cases/million people (based on studies published between 2011 and 2021). In Europe and the United States of America, cases are gener- ally classified as being community (60–70%), travel (20–25%) or hospital/nosocomial (5–10%) acquired. Host factors influence the likelihood of illness; males are more fre- quently affected than females, and most cases occur in people over 50 years of age. Risk factors associated with disease include smoking, diabetes, chronic respiratory disease, immunosuppression and excessive alcohol consumption. While disease is uncommon in the young, there have been cases in neonates associated with humidifiers and birth- ing pools. Legionellosis can occur at any time of year, but increased cases have been reported in the warmer months of summer and autumn. Most cases are sporadic, but outbreaks can occur, with the most common sources being cooling towers and hot and cold water systems in buildings and spas. Transmission The most common route of transmission of Legionella is the inhalation of contami- nated aerosols produced by devices linked to drinking-water systems. Aspiration of contaminated water is also a potential route of transmission. There is little evidence of person-to-person transmission. The infectivity of L. pneumophila is not known and

In some situations, the infective dose could be very low, as cases have been recorded following short exposure to Legionella . Growth within amoebae enhances the ability of Legionella to parasitize lung macrophages and cause disease. The incubation period for Legionnaires’ disease is generally 2–10 days. The incubation period for Pontiac fever is 5 hours–3 days. Detection methods Standard culture-based methods for Legionella are available. Serological and molecu- lar methods are also available (see section 7.4). Source and occurrence Legionella occur naturally in relatively low numbers in many freshwater environ- ments, such as groundwater, streams, rivers and reservoirs. Legionella may multi - ply in engineered water environments (e.g. drinking-water distribution systems) that provide conditions to support the survival and growth of Legionella in biofilms, particularly in association with free-living amoebae. Optimum growth temperatures for Legionella are 20–50 °C. Hot and cold water distribution systems in buildings, air-conditioning systems and spas are the most common sources of contaminated aerosols, but a range of devices or installations that produce mists or sprays can also be sources of Legionella. Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4), control measures to manage potential risks from Legio- nella should focus on a combination of strategies to limit their survival during treat- ment and their growth in biofilms, including in free-living amoebae in distribution systems and building water systems. Legionella are moderately resistant to oxidizing disinfectants such as chlorine, but doses typically used in drinking-water treatment plants should be sufficient to inactivate planktonic Legionella . UV light is also effec- tive against planktonic Legionella. Control strategies to reduce biofilm formation can reduce the potential for Legionella to survive and grow. Lastly, Legionella can be a particular concern in devices receiving drinking-water, such as cooling towers and hot water systems in large buildings; see section 6.10 for more information on man- aging water systems in buildings including temperature regulation and minimizing dissemination of aerosols. As Legionella is a non-faecal, environmental organism that can persist and grow in water, E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator for its possible presence or absence in drinking-water (see section 11.6). Leptospira Significance in drinking‑water Leptospira are of low health significance in drinking-water. The evidence linking transmission with ingestion of drinking-water is weak, with reported drinking-water

270 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA cases and outbreaks having been linked only to storage reservoirs contaminated due to accidents or disasters. Water-based leptospirosis is normally caused by skin contact with contaminated surface water, especially after extreme rain events or flooding. General description Leptospira are tightly coiled, spiral-shaped bacteria. Leptospira include more than 35 species that are divided into three clusters. The pathogenic and intermediate clusters include the disease-causing species such as L. interrogans. Human health effects The severity of illness and the symptoms associated with leptospirosis vary widely. Infections are often subclinical. Symptoms may include fever, headache, muscle pain, chills, red eyes, abdominal pain, jaundice, haemorrhages of skin and mucous mem- branes, vomiting, diarrhoea and skin rash. The illness may progress to kidney or liver failure, aseptic meningitis or pulmonary bleeding, which are life-threatening compli- cations. Long-lasting sequelae include depression, headaches, fatigue and joint pains. An acute and severe form of leptospirosis is known as Weil’s disease, which is charac- terized by jaundice, renal failure and enlargement of the spleen. Epidemiology Leptospirosis occurs globally, affecting people living in temperate and tropical cli- mates in rural and urban areas. Although the incidence of human infection is higher in tropical rather than temperate regions, transmission occurs in both high- and low- income countries. Seasonal peaks in disease incidence exist in most regions. In tropi- cal countries, epidemiological clusters of leptospirosis are observed following floods, storms and hurricanes. In temperate climates, leptospirosis is commonly linked to occupational activities or recreational waters. Leptospirosis is recognized as a disease with epidemic potential in many parts of the world. Transmission The major transmission route for Leptospira is through contact with infected animals or contact with water and soil contaminated with the urine of infected animals. Patho- genic Leptospira persist in the renal tubules of mammalian hosts, which may have chronic asymptomatic infections with excretion persisting for a very long time, po- tentially even lifelong. Rodents, insectivores, dogs, cattle and swine are considered to be the main reservoirs. Leptospira can enter the body through cuts and abrasions in the skin or via the mucous membranes of the mouth, nose and eyes. Ingestion of con- taminated food and water, or inhalation of aerosols, may occasionally cause infection, but it is not transmitted by the faecal–oral route. Person-to-person transmission is rarely observed. There is an increasing trend of outbreaks associated with recreational exposure to contaminated water. Outbreaks have also been associated with disasters involving flooding. Sexual contact, transplacental transmission and breast milk are potential routes of exposure. Infectivity of Leptospira varies depending on settings, exposure routes and human host status.

270 271 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Detection methods Culture-based and molecular methods are available for detection, quantification and typing of Leptospira in environmental samples (see section 7.4). Molecular methods are preferred since differentiation of pathogenic and non-pathogenic strains is more straightforward and reliable, and because biosafety concerns are lower, compared to culture methods. Source and occurrence There are limited data on occurrence of Leptospira , but they have been detected in water and wastewater environments including surface water with prevalence influ- enced by rainfall and contamination with urine and tissues of infected animals. Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4), control measures to manage potential risks from Lep - tospira include protection of source waters and storage reservoirs from urine and tissues of infected animals, application of adequate treatment processes and protec- tion of drinking-water quality during treated water distribution and storage from external contamination. Chlorine is an effective drinking-water disinfectant against Leptospira. As Leptospira is a non-faecal organism that can persist in water, E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator for its possible presence or absence in drinking-water. Non-tuberculous Mycobacterium Significance in drinking‑water There is moderate evidence for waterborne transmission of non-tuberculous Myco- bacterium (NTM). In a number of NTM disease investigations, the detection of NTM in drinking-water and the identified routes of transmission suggested that drinking- water supplies were a plausible source of infection. In addition, a number of outbreaks have been reported in health-care centres associated with a single facility or a specific procedure. General description Mycobacterium are Gram-positive, non-spore-forming, rod-shaped bacteria, with a thick, lipid-rich outer membrane. The family includes up to 200 species and 13 sub- species. The “typical” species of Mycobacterium, such as M. tuberculosis, M. bovis, M. africanum and M. leprae, have only human or animal reservoirs and are not transmit- ted by water. In contrast, the atypical or non-tuberculous species of Mycobacterium (NTM) are natural inhabitants of a variety of water and soil environments. Among the NTM, the most common cause of disease is the M. avium complex (M. avium , M. intracellulare and M. chimaera) followed by the M. abscessus complex, M. kansasii complex, M. malmoense, M. simiae and M. xenopi.

272 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Human health effects Mycobacterium are opportunistic pathogens. NTM infections are commonly asymp- tomatic, but can cause a broad range of diseases involving the skeleton, lymph nodes, skin and soft tissues, as well as the respiratory, gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts. The most common presentation is pulmonary disease; other manifestations include disseminated disease, lymphadenitis, skin ulcers, post-traumatic wound infec- tions and nosocomial disease. Disseminated infections are a common cause of death in HIV-positive persons. Due to their cell wall structure, NTM have a high resistance to antimicrobials, which complicates treatment. Epidemiology The worldwide incidence of NTM-mediated disease is unknown due to limited sur - veillance. Variation in disease presentation, lack of knowledge of diagnostic features and challenges with microbiological diagnosis contribute to uncertainty about inci- dence. However, there has been evidence (including from a 2021 study) of increasing prevalence of NTM-mediated disease in North America, Europe, Asia and Australia. Some species such as the M. avium complex and M. abscessus have worldwide sig- nificance, while others can be geographically limited. For example, M. malmoense is common in Europe, but rarely reported in the United States of America. However, compared to the widespread prevalence of the organism, disease is relatively infre- quent. Estimated annual incidence rates reported range from 1.0 to 9.8 cases/100 000 persons in high-income countries (based on studies published in 2007 and 2016). Host factors play a significant role in susceptibility to disease including immunodeficiency (e.g. HIV infection), organ transplant, inflammatory disorders, genetic background, and presence of localized or generalized lung damage (e.g. chronic obstructive pul- monary disease, cystic fibrosis). Transmission Principal routes of waterborne infection are inhalation of aerosols, contact with con- taminated materials or ingestion of contaminated water, primarily in health-care centres. Identifying sources of mycobacterial disease can be complicated by delays in diagnosis and microbial identification, but there is some evidence linking cases to or- ganisms in drinking-water. Processed water used for dialysis and bioaerosols from heating–cooling units used during cardiothoracic surgery have been linked to out- breaks. Occurrence of pseudo-outbreaks (increase in positive cultures without evi- dence of disease) and pseudo-infections can complicate the identification of sources of clinically relevant NTM. These pseudo-outbreaks are often caused by sample or equipment contamination by NTM from health-care water supplies, leading to con- tamination of equipment or ice. There is no evidence of person-to-person or zoonotic transmission of NTM, al- though indirect person-to-person transmission of M. abscessus between cystic fibro- sis patients has been suggested. The infective dose is not known and is likely to vary depending on the susceptibility of those exposed and the virulence of individual spe- cies and strains. The incubation period is unknown and probably varies depending on the nature of the disease, but can be weeks to months.

272 273 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Detection methods There are culture-based methods for detection of NTM although isolation can be challenging due to their slow growth in the environment and in culture media. Molecular methods are also available for detection and speciation (see section 7.4). Source and occurrence NTM are ubiquitous inhabitants of natural water and soil environments and can thrive in engineered water environments (e.g. drinking-water distribution systems) that provide conditions to support the survival and growth of NTM in biofilms, in- cluding in association with free-living amoebae. M. kansasii, M. xenopi and M. simiae are recovered almost exclusively from drinking-water. Optimum growth temperatures for NTM species vary, but growth is reduced at temperatures outside the range of 20–55 °C. Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4), control measures to manage potential risks from NTM should focus on a combination of strategies to limit their survival during treatment and their growth in biofilms including in free-living amoebae in distribution systems and building water systems. NTM are highly resistant to oxidizing disinfectants such as chlorine, but maintaining continuous levels of adequate disinfectant residuals in the distribution system and building water systems should reduce concentrations of planktonic NTM. Planktonic NTM are sensitive to UV light. Control strategies to reduce biofilm formation can reduce the potential for NTM to survive and grow. In a similar fashion to Legionella , NTM temperature regulation should be applied for building water systems to minimize growth of NTM; see section 6.10 for further information. As NTM is a non-faecal, environmental organism that can survive and grow in water and is highly resistant to chlorine, E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator for its possible presence or absence in drinking-water (see section 11.6). Pseudomonas aeruginosa Significance in drinking‑water Pseudomonas aeruginosa is of low health significance in drinking-water. Although P . aeruginosa can be detected in drinking-water, there is no evidence linking trans- mission with drinking-water for the general population. However, transmission of non-gastrointestinal infections by P . aeruginosa to susceptible patients in health-care facilities through drinking-water may be possible, with a limited number of hospital outbreaks having been reported due to use of contaminated water in patient care. The presence of high concentrations of P . aeruginosa can result in taste, odour and turbid- ity problems in drinking-water.

274 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA General description P . aeruginosa is a Gram-negative, motile, rod-shaped bacteria. There are about 200 Pseudomonas species, of which P . aeruginosa is most prominent as a potential con- cern to human health, especially strains that are antimicrobial resistant. Human health effects P . aeruginosa is an opportunistic pathogen, commonly causing pneumonia, especially in health-care facilities. Cystic fibrosis and immunocompromised patients are prone to respiratory tract colonization with P . aeruginosa, which may lead to serious progres- sive pulmonary infections and death. P . aeruginosa may also cause chronic infections in individuals with chronic obstructive pulmonary disorder. In addition, P . aeruginosa infects sites such as burns, surgical wounds and physically damaged eyes. It can infect individuals who are using catheters or other in-dwelling medical devices. It is also a major cause of urinary tract infections. From these sites, it may invade the body, caus- ing destructive lesions or septicaemia and meningitis. It rarely causes serious illness in healthy individuals without some predisposing factor. However, it can cause eye infections, especially among contact lens wearers, ear infections, skin infections and folliculitis associated with warm, recreational bathing waters. Epidemiology P . aeruginosa is one of the most important causes of illness and death due to bacterial infections, including those associated with antimicrobial resistance. Immunocompro- mised individuals and those with other predisposing factors are at highest risk of seri- ous illness. Transmission Transmission of P . aeruginosa in the general population is principally through contact with recreational water. Ingestion of community drinking-water has not been identi- fied as a source of infection. In health-care facilities, transmission can occur through aspiration of endogenous oral microbiota, aspiration from contaminated mechanical respiratory ventilators or other health-care devices, or through hematogenous spread. Physical contact with environmental sources such as water-associated fixtures, and cross-contamination in the health-care environment are also possible exposure routes. A limited number of hospital outbreaks have occurred due to contaminated water used for vulnerable patients including for enteral feeding, and to prepare medications. Two of three outbreaks were associated with bottled water/mineral water. The infec- tivity of P . aeruginosa for humans through ingestion is unknown, but based on a hu- man volunteer study, it is expected to be low. Detection methods Culture-based and biochemical methods are available for P . aeruginosa . Molecular methods are also available (see section 7.4). Source and occurrence P . aeruginosa is a common water and soil organism and is found frequently in source water. P . aeruginosa has also been detected in drinking-water. It can persist for long

274 275 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA periods (over 1 month at 20 °C) and multiply in water environments and on the sur - face of suitable organic materials in contact with water in biofilms. P . aeruginosa are important bacteria in biofilms in premise plumbing, especially of health-care facilities. They have been isolated from a range of moist environments, such as sinks, hot water systems, showers, bathtubs, pools and spas in health-care and community settings. Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4), control measures that effectively manage the presence and growth of bacteria in drinking-water supplies will control P . aeruginosa . These include application of adequate treatment processes and effective biofilm management in distribution systems and building water systems, including health-care facilities. WSPs for health-care facilities need to also consider the susceptibilities of patients. P. aeruginosa has low to moderate resistance to oxidizing disinfectants such as chlorine, but doses and contact times typically used in drinking-water treatment plants should be sufficient to inactivate planktonic P . aeruginosa. The presence of Pseudomonas in drinking-water supplies is generally considered a nuisance condition that could be indicative of inadequate management practices. As P . aeruginosa is an environmental organism and can persist and grow in water, E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator of its possible presence or absence in drinking-water. Salmonella – non-typhoidal Significance in drinking‑water Non-typhoidal Salmonella (NTS) is an important zoonotic waterborne pathogen, with strong evidence from a number of outbreaks linking transmission to drinking- water particularly involving untreated or poorly treated groundwater and small rain- water systems. General description Salmonella are Gram-negative, non-spore-forming, rod-shaped bacteria that are pre- dominantly motile. There are two species: S. enterica and S. bongori. S. enterica (sub- species enterica, salamae, arizonae, diarizonae, indica and houtenae) are associated with greater than 99% of Salmonella -caused diseases in humans and other warm- blooded animals. In addition to classification of subspecies, Salmonella are further subdivided into serovars. S. enterica subspecies enterica, serovar Typhi and Paratyphi are known as the typhoidal Salmonella serovars, whereas all other serovars are known as NTS. A large number of NTS serovars infect humans, with S. enterica subspecies enterica, serovars Typhimurium and Enteritidis being the most common causes of disease. Typhoidal Salmonella are the subject of a separate fact sheet. Human health effects In general, NTS presents less severe symptoms and lower mortality rates than infec- tion with the typhoidal serovars S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi. Characteristic gastrointes-

276 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA tinal symptoms of NTS include diarrhoea (which occasionally may be bloody), often accompanied by fever, abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. Symptoms are usually self-limiting but may persist for several days. Dehydration may be severe among vul- nerable patients. Death is uncommon in otherwise healthy individuals, but is more likely in vulnerable age groups, as well as in immunocompromised individuals. In addition to gastroenteritis, NTS has also been identified as a major cause of invasive disease (e.g. bacteraemia), particularly in Africa. As with some other gas- trointestinal infections, a small subset of patients with non-typhoidal salmonellosis may also develop post-infectious disease syndromes such as reactive arthritis, irri- table bowel syndrome and possibly inflammatory bowel disease. For severe cases of non-typhoidal salmonellosis, treatment with antibiotics may be recommended, but the prevalence of NTS resistant to multiple antibiotics is increasing. Prolonged carriers should not be treated with antibiotics. Epidemiology NTS is a common cause of diarrhoeal disease. However, in low-income, high-burden settings, NTS contributes only a small amount of the burden of childhood diarrhoeal disease compared with other enteric pathogens. Salmonellosis is most extensively reported in North America and Europe due to better surveillance systems. Invasive NTS is especially common in sub-Saharan Africa, where it has been identified as a leading cause of community-acquired blood stream infections. Transmission NTS is transmitted primarily by the faecal–oral (or urine–oral) route, with animals being the primary source. Food of animal origin is the most common source of sal- monellosis. S. Enteritidis is commonly associated with poultry and poultry products, whereas S. Typhimurium has a wider species range, including pigs, cattle and poul- try. An increasing number of illnesses have been associated with the consumption of fruits and vegetables. Transmission may also occur through ingestion of water contaminated with animal faeces, or by direct exposure to infected animals or their environments. Although documented cases are rare, person-to-person transmission may occur through direct contact or indirectly by pathogens from human faeces transferred on environmental surfaces or through unsafe handling of food. Direct person-to-person transmission is more likely to occur in infants and persons with certain underlying conditions. There are several estimates of the infectivity of NTS based on ingestion of food, which might not be applicable to drinking-water. An analysis of data from human feeding trials determined a dose associated with a 50% infection rate (ID 50) of 23 600 organisms, while ID50 values ranging from 7 to 9610 organisms were estimated based on analysis of foodborne outbreaks. Overall, based on these estimates, the relative infectivity of NTS by ingestion is considered moderate. Incubation periods are typi- cally 6–72 hours. Pathogen shedding occurs throughout the course of illness and may continue for varying periods afterwards. The median period of pathogen excretion is from 6 weeks to 3 months, depending on the serotype, but 1% of infected adults and 5% of infected children may excrete the pathogens for up to 1 year. Acquired immu- nity to NTS can develop to some extent, but invasive species may still cause infections.

276 277 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Detection methods Standard culture-based methods for NTS are available, as well as serological typing methods, immunoassays and molecular methods (see section 7.4). Source and occurrence NTS is found in a broad range of water and wastewater environments including sur - face water, vulnerable groundwater and drinking-water. Prevalence is influenced by the presence of faecal contamination including from human sewage (untreated or partially treated) and from animals. Persistence of NTS is expected to be moderate (1 week to 1 month at 20 °C), with survival influenced by sunlight, biotic factors and their ability to survive within amoebae. Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4), control measures to manage potential risks from NTS should include protection of source waters from contamination by human and animal faecal wastes (including extra vigilance during heavy rain), application of adequate water treatment processes and protection of drinking-water quality during distribu- tion. Drinking-water should be protected from faecal contamination by birds and other animals during storage. Chlorine and UV light are effective drinking-water dis- infectants against NTS. E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is a suitable indicator for the possible presence or absence of NTS in drinking-water (see section 11.6). Bibliography WHO (2025) Non-typhoidal Salmonella. Salmonella – typhoidal Significance in drinking‑water Typhoidal Salmonella (S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi) is a major waterborne pathogen with strong evidence from multiple outbreaks and endemic disease linking transmission to contaminated drinking-water. General description Salmonella are Gram-negative, non-spore-forming, rod-shaped bacteria that are pre- dominantly motile. There are two species: S. enterica and S. bongori. S. enterica (sub- species enterica, salamae, arizonae, diarizonae, indica and houtenae) are associated with greater than 99% of Salmonella -caused diseases in humans and other warm- blooded animals. In addition to classification of subspecies, Salmonella are further subdivided into serovars. S. enterica subspecies enterica, serovar Typhi (S. Typhi) and serovar Paratyphi (S. Paratyphi) are known as the typhoidal Salmonella for their re- spective abilities to cause typhoid and paratyphoid fevers in humans, whereas all other Salmonella are non-typhoidal (NTS). NTS are the subject of a separate fact sheet.

278 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Human health effects Severity of illness associated with S . Typhi varies from nonspecific illness to life- threatening typhoid fever. In endemic areas, many of those infected, particularly young children, may have a mild, nonspecific gastrointestinal disease that is not recog- nized clinically as typhoid fever. Initial symptoms of typhoid fever include headache, malaise, cough, diffuse abdominal pain, constipation and remittent fever, but patients may become progressively ill without treatment, and experience mental confusion, apathy with sustained fever and abdominal distension. Life-threatening complica- tions include intestinal haemorrhage and perforation. Surviving patients may experi- ence continuing weakness and persistent weight loss for months. Pneumonia, and joint and urinary tract infections are examples of atypical presentations of typhoid fever. Asymptomatic infection can also occur. Infection with S. Paratyphi causes simi- lar, although generally milder, symptoms. Resistance of typhoidal Salmonella to mul- tiple antibiotics emerged in the 1980s, and increasing resistance to fluoroquinolones has been reported. Epidemiology Typhoid fever is more prevalent than paratyphoid fever. The highest known rates of typhoid and paratyphoid fever are in south-east Asia and sub-Saharan Africa. The age distribution of illness from typhoid fever varies between endemic and low-prevalence settings. In endemic areas, illness is most common in children. In low-prevalence areas, the incidence has a more even age distribution, and a high proportion of cases are a result of travel to endemic disease areas. Transmission S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi are spread primarily by the faecal–oral (or urine–oral) route and are largely restricted to humans. Infection by typhoidal Salmonella is mostly as- sociated with the consumption of contaminated water and food. There is a strong association of typhoid and paratyphoid fever with inadequate sanitation, unsafe drinking-water and poor hygiene. In endemic areas, there is evidence that children contract S. Typhi from heavily contaminated environments through physical contact with water sources. Typhoid fever can occasionally be transmitted by direct person- to-person contact, but this is a less important route than contaminated food or water. The relative infectivity of S. Typhi is low, with an estimated dose associated with a 50% infection rate (ID 50) of 1.1 × 10 6 organisms. The incubation period is usually 8–14 days for typhoid fever and 1–10 days for paratyphoid fever. Patients excrete the pathogen throughout the period of symptomatic infections and for variable periods afterwards. For paratyphoid fever, shedding is common for 1–2 weeks after symp- toms. For about 10% of S . Typhi patients with no treatment, shedding can continue for 3 months after. Between 1% and 5% of patients become chronic carriers without ongoing symptoms and excrete the pathogen for more than a year. A partial form of immunity may follow recovery from symptomatic and asymptomatic infection. Detection methods Standard culture-based methods for S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi are available, as well as serological typing methods, immunoassays and molecular methods (see section 7.4).

278 279 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Source and occurrence There are limited data on the occurrence of S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi, but they have been detected in water and wastewater environments including surface water and in- adequately treated drinking-water. Prevalence is influenced by the presence of human faecal waste including from sewage (untreated or partially treated). Persistence in water is short (up to 1 week at 20 °C). Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4), control measures to manage potential risks from S. Ty- phi and S. Paratyphi should include protection of source waters from contamination by human faecal waste (including extra vigilance during heavy rain), application of adequate water treatment processes and protection of drinking-water quality during storage and distribution. Chlorine and UV light are effective drinking-water disinfec- tants against typhoidal Salmonella. E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is a suitable indicator for the possible presence or absence of S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi in drinking- water (see section 11.6). Shigella Significance in drinking‑water Shigella are major waterborne pathogens, with strong evidence from multiple out- breaks linking transmission to contaminated drinking-water. General description Shigella are Gram-negative, non-spore-forming, non-motile, rod-like bacteria. There are four species of Shigella: S. dysenteriae, S. flexneri, S. boydii and S. sonnei, which are further divided into a number of serotypes. Although Shigella are classified in a sepa- rate genus, they are genetically very similar to pathogenic E. coli. It is generally consid- ered that Shigella belong to the same pathotype as enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC), but are more virulent. EIEC is the subject of the separate diarrhoeagenic E. coli fact sheet. Human health effects Shigella can cause mild to serious illness, including bacillary dysentery (shigellosis). The severity and case fatality vary by species and serotype, as well as host charac- teristics. Abdominal cramps, fever, watery diarrhoea and dehydration occur early in the infection. Illness due to S. sonnei is usually relatively mild and self-limiting. Shiga toxin-producing S. dysenteriae type 1 is most often associated with severe disease and associated complications, including toxic megacolon, intestinal perforations and haemolytic uraemic syndrome. Long-term complications in children infected with S. dysenteriae in low- and middle-income countries include persistent diarrhoea, with severe dehydration and malnutrition, while children hospitalized with shigellosis fre- quently experience seizures. S. flexneri has been associated with infectious arthritis.

280 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Death from shigellosis is most likely in young children and elderly people. A high in- cidence of resistance of Shigella to all first-line antibiotics has been reported; therefore, treatment options for Shigella-mediated dysentery are becoming limited. Epidemiology Shigella are one of the most common causes of moderate to severe diarrhoea and death, including among young children in low- and middle-income countries. Sea- sonal fluctuations of shigellosis occur that vary between settings. S. dysenteriae type 1 pandemics have resulted in high rates of fatalities for all age groups in Central Amer- ica, South Asia, and Central and East Africa. The four Shigella species have differ - ent distributions: S. dysenteriae is mainly found in South America, Africa and Asia, S. flexneri in low-income countries with endemic shigellosis, S. boydii in India and S. sonnei in high-income countries. Transmission Shigella are transmitted primarily by the faecal–oral route through person-to-person contact, and by ingestion of contaminated food or water. Humans and other higher primates appear to be the only natural hosts for Shigella . The risk of transmission is greatest in low-income settings where sanitation and hygiene conditions are gener - ally poor, with sporadic cases and outbreaks of shigellosis often occurring in crowded communities or institutions, including day-care centres and health-care facilities. Cases and outbreaks have also been associated with recreational waters. Flies have also been identified as a transmission vector from contaminated faecal waste. The relative infectivity varies among the species. S. dysenteriae is highly infec- tive with an estimated dose associated with a 50% infection rate (ID 50) of 36 organ- isms. S. flexneri is moderately infective, with an estimated ID50 of 148 organisms. The incubation period ranges between 1 and 3 days, but may be up to 1 week, depending on the species and the host. The pathogen is usually shed for up to 4 weeks upon illness and following recovery; in in rare cases, it can be shed for months. Repeated exposure to Shigella can provide protective immunity. Detection methods Standard culture-based methods for Shigella are available, but they are complex. In addition, commercial biochemical tests to type isolates exist. Molecular methods are also available (see section 7.4). Source and occurrence There are limited data on the occurrence of Shigella due to challenges in detecting these pathogens in environmental samples. Nevertheless, they have been detected in water and wastewater environments, including surface water, vulnerable groundwater and inadequately treated drinking-water. Prevalence is influenced by the presence of sewage (untreated or partially treated). Based on limited studies, the persistence of Shigella in water is likely to be moderate (1 week to 1 month at 20 °C). Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4 ), control measures to manage the potential risks from Shigella should include protection of source waters from contamination by human

Chlorine and UV light are effective drinking-water disinfectants against Shigella. E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is a suitable indicator for the possible presence or absence of Shigella in drinking-water (see section 11.6). Bibliography WHO (2025) Shigella. Staphylococcus aureus Significance in drinking‑water Staphylococcus aureus is of low health significance in drinking-water. Although it has been detected in drinking-water, there is no evidence linking transmission with this source. Infections of susceptible individuals in health-care facilities through drinking- water may be possible, but have not been identified. General description S. aureus is a non-motile, non-spore-forming, Gram-positive round-shaped bacterium. The Staphylococcus genus contains at least 47 different species, of which only S. aureus, S. epidermidis , S. saprophyticus, S. haemolyticus, S. lugdunensis and S. argenteus are associated with disease in humans. Human health effects S. aureus is an opportunistic pathogen, and some strains are common human com- mensal organisms. It can affect healthy and vulnerable populations. Methicillin- resistant S. aureus causes more serious human health effects than methicillin-sensitive S. aureus, but both can be pathogenic. S. aureus skin and soft tissue infections are com- mon and typically occur as pimples, furuncles, carbuncles and folliculitis. Multiplica- tion in tissues can result in boils, skin sepsis, septicaemia, endocarditis, osteomyelitis, urinary tract infections and pneumonia. In health-care facilities, S. aureus can cause various invasive infections. The onset of clinical symptoms for these infections is rela- tively long, usually several days. S. aureus can also produce extracellular enzymes and toxins that commonly cause foodborne intoxications as well as clinical toxinoses such as toxic shock syndrome, septic shock and scalded skin syndrome. Epidemiology S. aureus, especially methicillin-resistant S. aureus, is an important cause of pneu- monia and other serious and life-threatening diseases in community and health-care settings. It is one of the most important causes of death due to bacterial infections, including those associated with antimicrobial resistance. Transmission S. aureus is not transmitted by the faecal–oral route. Person-to-person contact (hand- to-hand and other skin-to-skin contact) or contact with contaminated fomites are the most common routes of transmission. Community-acquired exposures are more

282 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA likely when hygienic conditions are inadequate due to crowding, or where there is inadequate access to sanitation and poor personal hygiene, such as lack of handwash- ing access and practices, and sharing of towels, clothing, razors, unwashed bedding and intravenous drug use. Hospitals and other health-care facilities are also major reservoirs and exposure sources of methicillin-resistant S. aureus. Infected patients can transmit these bacteria person to person, from shed human skin and also release them to the environment via hospital wastewater discharges. Foodborne intoxication risks from S. aureus are also common, with outbreaks reported globally. Close contact with livestock is another source of exposure to methicillin-resistant and methicillin- sensitive S. aureus. The infectivity of S. aureus through ingestion is unknown. Detection methods Culture-based methods are available for S. aureus. Molecular methods are also avail- able and used in clinical diagnostic analysis and epidemiological investigations (see section 7.4). Source and occurrence S. aureus is widespread in soil and water environments and has been detected in source waters. S. aureus is frequently detected in unchlorinated drinking-water at rela- tively low concentrations. It has also been detected in inadequately treated drinking- water. Concentrations can be higher in water from faucets with aerators, presumably due to human contact, colonization and biofilm formation. S. aureus can persist for long periods in water (over 1 month at 20 °C). Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4), control measures that effectively manage the presence and growth of bacteria in drinking-water supplies will control S. aureus. These in- clude application of adequate treatment processes and effective biofilm management in distribution systems and building water systems, including health-care facilities. WSPs for health-care facilities need to also consider the susceptibilities of patients. Chlorine is an effective drinking-water disinfectant against S. aureus. As S. aureus is a non-faecal, environmental and commensal organism that can persist and grow in water, E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator for its possible presence or absence in drinking-water. Tsukamurella Significance in drinking‑water Tsukamurella are of low health significance in drinking-water. Although they have been detected in drinking-water, there is no evidence linking transmission with this source. Infection of susceptible individuals through drinking-water may be possible, but it has not been identified.

282 283 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA General description Tsukamurella are Gram-positive, obligate bacteria with varying morphologies from straight to curved rods. There are about 14 species, with some associated with human infections including T. tyrosinosolvens, T. hongkongensis, T. inchonensis, T. pseudo- spumae, T. paurometabola, T. pulmonis, T. sinensis, T. soli, T. spumae and T. strandjordae. Human health effects Tsukamurella can cause respiratory infections and chronic lung diseases such as pneu- monia and tuberculosis-like disease, bacteraemia, meningitis and brain abscesses, peritonitis, keratitis, conjunctivitis, cutaneous infections and acute otitis media. Epidemiology Most Tsukamurella infections are hospital associated. Risk factors for infection and illness include other predisposing health conditions, such as immunosuppression due to HIV/AIDS, cancer and immunosuppressive therapies, renal failure and exposure to contaminated medical equipment and materials. Community-acquired pneumonia has been reported, but is rare. Cases have been reported in Europe, Asia, America and Africa, although the disease burden from Tsukamurella is thought to be relatively low compared to other causes of the same diseases or syndromes in at-risk populations, usually in health-care facilities. Transmission Tsukamurella are not transmitted by the faecal–oral route. In health-care facilities, person-to-person contact through direct contact with wounds or contact with con- taminated fomites are the likely transmission pathways for susceptible individuals. In community-acquired cases, sources of infection are typically not identified. In hos- pital and community-acquired cases, the original sources of infecting Tsukamurella are often not known, but may be environmental or humans and animal hosts. The infectivity of Tsukamurella is unknown. However, the widespread occurrence of Tsu- kamurella in the environment and their low disease burden in healthy people suggest relatively low infectivity. Detection methods Tsukamurella are recoverable by the heterotrophic plate count method. They are also recoverable by selective media for aerobic actinomycetes. Definitive identification in clinical diagnostic laboratories is based on molecular analysis (see section 7.4). Source and occurrence As actinomycetes, Tsukamurella are widespread in soil and water environments in- cluding surface water, and have been detected in drinking-water. As Tsukamurella are known to proliferate in the environment and survive in biofilms, they are expected to persist in water for long periods (over 1 month at 20 °C). Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4), control measures that effectively manage the presence and growth of bacteria in drinking-water supplies and building water systems will control Tsukamurella. These include application of adequate treatment processes and

284 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA effective biofilm management in distribution systems and building water systems in- cluding health-care facilities. WSPs for health-care facilities need to also consider the susceptibilities of patients. Based on studies with other actinomycetes, Tsukamurella are likely to be moderately resistant to chlorine, but doses and contact times typi- cally used in drinking-water treatment plants should provide adequate inactivation of planktonic Tsukamurella. As Tsukamurella are non-faecal environmental organ- isms that can persist and grow in water, E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator for their possible presence or absence in drinking-water. Bibliography WHO (2025) Tsukamurella. Background document for the WHO Guidelines for drinking-water quality. Geneva, World Health Organization. Vibrio cholerae Significance in drinking‑water Vibrio cholerae is a major waterborne pathogen, with strong evidence from epidemics and endemic areas linking transmission to drinking-water. Consumption of drinking- water contaminated with sewage is a primary source of V . cholerae. General description V . cholerae are small, motile, curved, Gram-negative rod-shaped bacteria. V . cholerae are classified into serogroups based on their O antigens with a limited number able to produce cholera enterotoxin. Only strains of serogroups O1 and O139 cause epi- demics. V . cholerae serogroup O1 can be divided into “classical” and “El Tor” biotypes based on phenotypic or biochemical characteristics. Each O1 biotype is further clas- sified into Ogawa, Inaba and Hikojima serotypes, with the Ogawa serotype being the most dominant serotype in cholera endemic areas. Human health effects Most infections caused by toxigenic V . cholerae are asymptomatic or result in mild symptoms. However, it can cause severe disease. There is no difference in the types of symptoms elicited by the different toxigenic strains of V . cholerae, but some El Tor O1 variants can cause more severe symptoms presumably due to the production of greater amounts of toxin. Non-toxin-producing strains of V . cholerae can cause self-limiting gastroenteritis, wound infections and bacteraemia. Host factor characteristics can also influence the severity of disease. The initial symptoms of cholera are an increase in peristalses followed by loose, watery and mucus-flecked “rice-water” stools. Complications of cholera are mainly attributed to dehydration and electrolyte loss, which may be accompanied by muscle cramps and seizures. Severe complications include acute renal failure, stroke, miscar- riages, premature deliveries and stillbirths. A substantially high percentage of untreat- ed cholera patients may die from the disease (more than 50% according to a 2017 review), but well-established diarrhoeal disease control programmes can reduce case fatality rates to less than 1%. The prevalence of V . cholerae resistant to multiple anti- biotics is steadily increasing. It is recommended that antibiotics should only be used in cholera cases with severe dehydration.

284 285 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Epidemiology V . cholerae is among the leading causes of diarrhoeal deaths globally. The majority of cases occur in Africa and south-east Asia. Cholera can be endemic, epidemic or pandemic. Epidemics are usually triggered by exogenous introduction of toxigenic V. cholerae and can be associated with disasters including floods, earthquakes, wars and other events that disrupt infrastructure and public health facilities. Climate change could increase the prevalence and severity of disrupting events. In endemic settings, the highest cholera incidence is among young children, with initial infection leading to immunity. When cholera epidemics occur in non-endemic populations, all ages lack pre-existing immunity, hence incidence rates of cholera are usually age indepen- dent. Prior infection by serotype-homogenous strains can provide partial immunity for at least 3 years. Exposure to El Tor Inaba cholera is partially protective against El Tor Ogawa cholera, but this cross-protection is not apparent in reverse, and no cross-protection has been detected between O1 and O139 strains. In cholera endemic countries, cases tend to occur seasonally, with one or two peaks per year depending on the country. The underlying basis for seasonality of cholera has not been deter - mined, but suggested factors include temperature, rainfall and plankton blooms. Transmission Transmission of toxigenic V . cholerae occurs by the faecal–oral route through inges- tion of contaminated water or food, with water the primary source of disease in en- demic areas. Use of this water for drinking, cooking, bathing and washing can lead to infection. Person-to-person transmission can occur within families, communities, institutional settings and crowded camps, particularly where sanitation and hygiene are poor. Toxigenic V . cholerae has been detected in domestic and farm animals, but there is no evidence that these animals are a source of infection. The relative infectivity is low in healthy people, with an estimated dose associ- ated with a 50% infection rate (ID 50) of 6.4 × 10 8 organisms, but infectivity can be moderate to low in people with reduced gastric acidity (ID 50 of 2.4 × 10 2 organisms). The incubation period is usually 18 hours–5 days. Symptomatic cases generally ex- crete the bacteria for only a few days after recovery, while asymptomatic cases may excrete the bacteria for 7–14 days. Chronic carriage is rare, although intermittent shedding can occur for several months. Detection methods Standard culture-based methods are available for V . cholerae. Species can be further characterized using biochemical and serological tests. Molecular methods are also available for detection of virulence factors including cholera toxin genes. Other meth- ods, incorporating immunofluorescence have also been developed to detect toxigenic strains (see section 7.4). Source and occurrence The occurrence of toxigenic V . cholerae in wastewaters and source waters, particularly surface waters, is correlated with occurrence of disease, but there have only been a few reports of detection in drinking-water. There are also few reports on the occurrence of V . cholerae in groundwater. V . cholerae can persist for moderate to long periods in

286 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA water (1 week to over 1 month at 20 °C) due to a variety of adaptive responses that increase resistance to stressors including nutrient limitation, predation and changes in salinity, temperature and pH. V . cholerae can survive in biofilms, assume “persister” phenotypes and switch from a smooth to a more robust “rugose” (wrinkled) variant. V . cholerae can also enter a viable but non-culturable state, but the mechanism of re- suscitation following ingestion and the epidemiological importance of the viable but non-culturable state is uncertain. Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4), control measures to manage potential risk from V. ch ol- erae should include protection of source waters from human faecal waste, applica- tion of adequate water treatment processes, and protection of drinking-water quality during storage and distribution. Control strategies to reduce biofilm formation can also reduce the potential for V . cholerae to survive in distribution systems. Chlorine and UV light are effective drinking-water disinfectants against V . cholerae. E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator for the absence of V . cholerae in drinking-water due to its long persistence. However, the presence of E. coli is a suit- able indicator of the possible presence of V . cholerae (see section 11.6). Bibliography WHO (2025) Vibrio cholerae. Y ersinia enterocolitica Significance in drinking‑water There is moderate evidence for waterborne transmission of Yersinia enterocolitica . Limited outbreaks have been reported from inadequately or non-disinfected small- scale drinking-water supplies. Untreated drinking-water has also been identified as a risk factor for sporadic Y. enterocolitica infections. General description Yersinia are Gram-negative, rod-shaped bacteria that are motile at temperatures of 22–29 °C, but become non-motile at normal human body temperature. The species Y. pestis, Y. pseudotuberculosis and certain serotypes of Y. enterocolitica are pathogenic for humans. While Y. enterocolitica is the dominant cause of enteric yersiniosis, Y. pseudotuberculosis can be responsible for extra-intestinal yersiniosis. Y. pestis is the cause of bubonic plague through contact with rodents and their fleas. Human health effects Infection with Y. enterocolitica can produce a range of clinical outcomes, although yer- siniosis generally presents as a self-limiting gastrointestinal infection. Severe yersini- osis generally presents as acute gastroenteritis with or without diarrhoea (which may be bloody), fever and abdominal pain. Clinical symptoms may also include acute in- flammation of the mesenteric lymph nodes mimicking appendicitis, inflammation of the pharynx and bacteraemia. More rarely, a range of non-gastrointestinal infections

286 287 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA such as abscesses, pyomyositis, pneumonia, meningitis, urinary tract infection, septic arthritis and conjunctivitis may occur. Post-infection complications include skin rash and reactive arthritis. Antibiotics may be used in severe cases involving systemic in- fections or invasive complications. Resistance to antibiotics in Y. enterocolitica varies among the different biotypes, but generally remains low with some exceptions. Epidemiology Detection of yersiniosis has primarily been limited to high-income countries, where it is an important cause of foodborne bacterial gastrointestinal illness. However, Y. enterocolitica has also been detected in humans and animals in low-income settings, although their significance is less well understood in these regions because of a lack of foodborne disease surveillance. Children appear to be more susceptible to infection; diarrhoea and abdominal pain seem to be more acute in children than in adults. Transmission Y. enterocolitica is transmitted primarily by the faecal–oral route. Wild and domestic animals, pigs in particular, are the principal reservoirs for infectious Y. enterocolitica. The major source of infection is considered to be contaminated food, particularly meat and meat products from pigs, but outbreaks from contaminated vegetables have been reported. Ingestion of contaminated drinking-water and contact with infected animals are also considered as potential risk factors for infection. The relative infectivity of Y. enterocolitica is unknown, but it is considered to be low with an estimated dose associated with a 50% infection rate (ID 50) of 109 organ- isms. Direct person-to-person transmission is therefore unlikely. The incubation period for yersiniosis in humans is usually under 10 days. Symptoms usually last for 2–3 weeks, and pathogens are shed in faeces for this period. Untreated cases may shed pathogens for 2–3 months, and long-term asymptomatic carriage can occur. Detection methods Culture-based methods are available, but they lack sensitivity and selectivity, which is likely to contribute to a substantial underestimation of the presence of pathogenic Y. enterocolitica in the environment. Molecular methods are also available (see sec - tion 7.4). Source and occurrence Y. enterocolitica is a common soil and water organism, and has been detected in sur - face water, groundwater and inadequately treated drinking-water. Prevalence is influ- enced primarily by the presence of animal faecal material, particularly from pigs. The presence of human faecal waste including sewage (untreated or partially treated) may also be a contributing factor. Limited studies suggest that Y. enterocolitica can survive for long periods in surface water (over 1 month at 20 °C). The presence of free-living amoeba and formation of biofilms have been shown to enhance their survival. Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4 ), control measures to manage potential risks from Y. enterocolitica should include protection of source waters from contamination by animal (particularly from pigs) and human faecal wastes, application of adequate

288 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA water treatment processes, and protection of drinking-water quality during storage and distribution. Control strategies to reduce biofilm formation can also reduce the potential for Y. enterocolitica to survive and grow in distribution systems. Chlorine and UV light are effective drinking-water disinfectants against Y. enterocolitica. Since some strains of Y. enterocolitica are environmental organisms and can persist and grow in water, the absence of E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator for its absence in drinking-water. However, the presence of E. coli is a suit- able indicator for the possible presence of Y. enterocolitica (see section 11.6). Bibliography WHO (2025) Y ersinia enterocolitica.
