Geneva, World Health Organization. 11.2 Viral pathogens Viruses with moderate to strong evidence of waterborne transmission are predomi- nantly enteric pathogens. With the exception of hepatitis E virus, humans are the only established source of human infectious species. However, zoonotic transmission may be possible for adenoviruses, noroviruses, rotaviruses and sapoviruses. Enteric viruses are typically transmitted by ingestion of contaminated drinking-water. Although in- fection is typically initiated by replication in the gastrointestinal tract, the illnesses caused by enteric viruses are more diverse than those caused by enteric bacteria and protozoa. For example, enteroviruses can cause mild illness characterized by cough, rash and fever through to a broad spectrum of diseases such as aseptic meningitis, encephalitis and poliomyelitis, while hepatitis A and E viruses can cause infectious hepatitis. For further information, including an overview of treatment considerations for viruses, see section 7.2.2. Adenoviruses Significance in drinking‑water Human adenoviruses (HAdVs) are important waterborne pathogens, with outbreaks primarily associated with recreational waters. HAdVs have been detected in substan- tial numbers in drinking-water and represent a likely but unconfirmed source of infec- tion. HAdVs are also considered important because they are among the most resistant waterborne pathogens to UV light. General description HAdVs consist of a double-stranded deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) genome in a non- enveloped icosahedral capsid that is about 90–100 nm in diameter. The family Adeno- viridae is classified into five recognized genera: Mastadenovirus with mammalian hosts, Aviadenovirus with avian hosts, and Atadenovirus, Ichtadenovirus and Siadeno- virus with a broad range of non-human hosts. HAdVs have been classified into seven species (A to G) and are further classified into 68 distinct types.

288 289 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Human health effects HAdVs cause a wide range of infections with a spectrum of clinical manifestations. Adenovirus types 40 and 41 (species F) are the most common associated with infec- tions of the gastrointestinal tract (gastroenteritis), especially in infants and children. Other types are associated with infections of the respiratory tract, the urinary tract and the eyes. HAdV infection can occasionally be fatal. Many infections are asymp- tomatic. Epidemiology Adenovirus infections have been detected worldwide. There have been numerous outbreaks associated with hospitals, military establishments, child-care centres and schools. In low-income settings, adenovirus types 40 and 41 have been identified as an important cause of diarrhoeal disease among young children. In addition to young children, immunocompromised individuals and elderly people are at risk of more se- vere disease. Infections occur year-round, with no marked seasonality. Transmission HAdV infections typically spread via person-to-person contact; this can include faecal–oral, oral–oral and hand–eye contact transmission. Inhalation of airborne viruses, ingesting contaminated recreational water and contact with contaminated fomites can also play a role in transmission. The consumption of contaminated food or drinking-water may be an important source of enteric illness, although there is no substantial evidence supporting these routes of transmission. Adenoviruses are gener- ally only pathogenic to the species of origin, but there is some evidence of zoonotic transmission. HAdVs are highly infective, with an estimated dose associated with a 50% infec- tion rate (ID 50) of 0.74 virus particles. The incubation period for HAdV-associated disease is 2–14 days. Individuals infected with enteric adenoviruses shed higher con- centrations of virus particles in faeces than those infected with non-enteric adeno- viruses. Shedding can continue for months after symptoms resolve. Serotype-specific immunity is conferred following infection with enteric adenoviruses, but this wanes over time. Detection methods Cell culture and molecular methods for HAdVs are available (see section 7.4). How- ever, some serotypes, including serotypes 40 and 41 are not readily isolated by cell cul- ture methods. Combining cell culture infectivity and molecular methods may improve the detection of infectious HAdVs. Source and occurrence HAdVs are found in a broad range of water and wastewater environments, and have been frequently detected in surface waters and treated drinking-water supplies. Preva- lence is influenced by the presence of human faeces including sewage (untreated or partially treated). HAdVs can persist for long periods in water (over 1 month at 20 °C).

290 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4 ), control measures to manage potential risks from HAdVs should include protection of source waters from contamination by human faecal waste, application of adequate water treatment processes, and protection of drinking-water quality during storage and distribution. Reduction of HAdVs by drinking-water treatment varies depending on the process. Chlorine is an effective drinking-water disinfectant, but UV light at commonly used doses is ineffective. Due to the smaller size of HAdVs relative to E.coli resulting in lower removal by treatment processes such as filtration, and their greater environmental persistence, the absence of E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator for their absence in drinking-water. However, the presence of E.coli is a suitable indicator for the possible presence of HAdVs (see section 11.6). Bibliography WHO (2025) Adenoviruses. Background document for the WHO Guidelines for drinking- water quality and the WHO Guidelines on sanitation and health. Geneva, World Health Organization. Aichiviruses Significance in drinking‑water Human aichiviruses (HAiVs) are of low health significance in drinking-water. Al- though HAiVs are transmitted by the faecal–oral route and have been detected in drinking-water, the evidence linking transmission with drinking-water is weak. General description Aichiviruses are small (30 nm in diameter) and consist of a single-stranded ribo- nucleic acid (RNA) genome in a non-enveloped capsid. There are six species of aichi- viruses (A to F) that can infect a broad range of animals. Aichivirus A is further divided into six types, one of which infects humans. Within HAiVs, three genotypes have been described (A, B and C). HAiV infection was first reported in 1989 in Japan. A retrospective study in archival samples dated its presence to July 1987 in sewage in the Netherlands. Human health effects Clinical symptoms of HAiV infection are similar to gastroenteritis, and include diar - rhoea, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and fever. The majority of individuals in- fected with HAiVs remain asymptomatic. Epidemiology HAiVs have been detected in human faecal samples in Africa, Asia, Europe and South America, suggesting that they are distributed worldwide. However, the epidemiology of gastroenteritis caused by HAiVs remains largely unknown. Transmission HAiVs can be transmitted by the faecal–oral route through ingestion of contaminated food, particularly shellfish. Transmission through ingestion of drinking-water is plau-

290 291 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA sible, but has not been confirmed. The relative infectivity of HAiVs is unknown, but given their similarities to other enteric viruses, it is expected to be high. Detection methods Cell culture and molecular methods are available for HAiV (see section 7.4). Source and occurrence Aichiviruses have been detected in a broad range of water and wastewater environ- ments. They have been found in surface water, groundwater and in one study of drinking-water. Prevalence is influenced by the presence of human faeces including sewage (untreated or partially treated). The persistence of HAiVs in water is un- known, but as they are resistant to environmental stress and based on similarities with other non-enveloped viruses, it is expected to be long (over 1 month at 20 °C). Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4 ), control measures to reduce potential microbial risks should be effective against HAiV . These include protection of source waters from con- tamination by human faecal waste, application of adequate water treatment processes, and protection of drinking-water quality during storage and distribution. Reduction of HAiVs by drinking-water treatment varies depending on the process. Based on their known resistance to environmental stress, HAiVs are likely to be moderately resistant to disinfection with chlorine, but doses and contact times typically used in drinking-water treatment should provide adequate inactivation. Due to the smaller size of HAiVs relative to E. coli, resulting in lower removal by treatment processes such as filtration, and their expected environmental persistence, the absence of E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator of their absence in drinking- water. However, the presence of E. coli is a suitable indicator of the possible presence of HAiVs (see section 11.6). Bibliography WHO (2025) Aichiviruses. Background document for the WHO Guidelines for drinking-water quality. Geneva, World Health Organization. Astroviruses Significance in drinking‑water Human astroviruses (HAstVs) are of low significance in drinking-water. Although HAstVs are transmitted by the faecal–oral route and have been detected in drinking- water, there is only weak evidence linking transmission with drinking-water. General description Astroviruses are small (28–35 nm in diameter) and consist of a single-stranded RNA genome with a non-enveloped icosahedral capsid. A proportion of astroviruses have a distinct star-shaped surface structure. There are human and animal strains with eight different serotypes of human astroviruses. Human astrovirus serotype 1 (HAstV-1) is the most commonly identified of these serotypes. Two novel groups of highly diver - gent HAstVs have also been identified.

292 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Human health effects HAstVs cause short-term, self-limiting diarrhoea with fever, abdominal pain and dehydration. Asymptomatic infection also occurs. Symptoms are generally mild and resolve without treatment within 2–3 days. In rare cases, severe central nervous sys- tem disease develops with high mortality rates in severely immunocompromised hu- man hosts. Epidemiology The global burden of HAstVs is unknown. HAstVs affect children worldwide, with limited reports of disease in normally healthy adults. However, immunocompromised individuals and elderly people are at high risk. Geographically, astroviruses are wide- spread. Although HAstV-1 is the most common, other serotypes are also widely dis- tributed with some geographical differences. In temperate regions, HAstV infections are higher in winter, while in tropical regions, infections peak in the rainy season. Transmission Human astroviruses are transmitted by the faecal–oral route, with person-to-person spread as the most common route of exposure. Contaminated food and fomites have also been identified as exposure sources. Transmission through ingestion of drinking- water is plausible but has not been confirmed. The relative infectivity of HAstVs is unknown, but given their similarities to other enteric viruses, it is probably high. Detection methods Cell culture and molecular methods are available for HAstVs (see section 7.4). Source and occurrence Astroviruses have been detected in a broad range of water and wastewater environ- ments, and have been often found in surface water. Astroviruses have also been de- tected in groundwater and drinking-water. Prevalence is influenced by the presence of human faeces including sewage (untreated or partially treated). HAstVs can persist for long periods in water (over 1 month at 20 °C). Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4 ), control measures to reduce potential microbial risks should be effective against HAstVs. These include protection of source waters from contamination by human faecal waste, application of adequate water treatment processes, and protection of drinking-water quality during storage and distribution. Reduction of HAstVs by drinking-water treatment varies depending on the process. Although HAstVs are moderately resistant to disinfection with chlorine, doses and contact times typically used in drinking-water treatment should provide adequate inactivation. Due to the smaller size of HAstVs relative to E. coli, resulting in lower removal by treatment processes such as filtration and their longer environmental persistence, the absence of E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator of their absence in drinking-water. However, the presence of E. coli is a suitable indicator of the possible presence of HAstVs.

Coronaviruses Significance in drinking‑water Coronaviruses are of low health significance in drinking-water. There is currently no evidence linking transmission with drinking-water. Furthermore, evidence suggests that drinking-water is an unlikely route of transmission. General description Coronaviruses have a single-stranded RNA genome in an enveloped nucleocapsid with a diameter of 50–200 nm. Coronaviridae is a family of mammalian and avian viruses with two subfamilies: Torovirinae and Coronavirinae. Most human corona- viruses are in the Coronavirinae subfamily, which has four genera: Alphacoronavi - rus (human coronaviruses 229E and NL63); Betacoronavirus (human coronaviruses HKU1 and OC43; Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus (MERS-CoV); severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus (SARS-CoV-1) and (SARS-CoV-2)); Deltacoronavirus (porcine coronavirus HKU15); and Gammacoronavirus (no human viruses). Principal hosts are birds and mammals, especially bats, but also other ani- mals such as swine, camels, civets and minks. Human health effects Coronavirus respiratory illnesses range from mild to fatal, including the common cold (caused by human coronaviruses OC43, 229E, HKU1 and NL63), pneumonia and respiratory distress syndromes. The most serious illnesses are SARS (caused by SARS-CoV-1), COVID-19 (caused by SARS-CoV-2) and MERS (caused by MERS- CoV). Asymptomatic or subclinical infections also occur. Long-term effects can oc- cur for some coronaviruses, particularly from COVID-19, with common symptoms of fatigue, attention disorder and laboured breathing. Epidemiology The epidemiology differs significantly by virus, with human coronaviruses 229E and OC43 being largely endemic in communities and hospital patients with respiratory illness. Coronaviruses causing SARS, MERS and COVID-19 have been characterized by epidemics and global pandemics of severe disease, with substantially higher case fatality rates than the common cold coronaviruses. Risk groups for more severe dis- ease associated with the common cold coronaviruses, MERS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2 include immunocompromised individuals and elderly people. Those with underly- ing diseases are also at increased risk for severe illness from coronaviruses causing MERS and COVID-19. There are seasonal peaks in winter for the common cold coronaviruses, and co-infections with other respiratory viruses are common.

294 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Transmission SARS-CoV-1, SARS-CoV-2 and MERS-CoV coronaviruses are zoonotic in origin, followed primarily by person-to-person respiratory spread. Hospitals and close con- tact settings with poor ventilation have been important in propagating outbreaks. Health-care workers are especially at risk of secondary infection. The relative infectiv- ity of SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2 is considered high. Inhalation of the virus from aerosolized faecal droplets has been linked to one outbreak of SARS and another of COVID-19. The droplets were generated from un- treated sewage in faulty plumbing systems of a residential building where an infected individual was present. These outbreaks were unique, with design characteristics of the building sewage and air handling systems contributing to possible but unproven transmission. Outbreaks transmitted through food or water have not been docu- mented. There is greater potential for environmental transmission via surfaces and fomites as potential sources of hand contamination, particularly where there is inad- equate hygiene and poor sanitation. Detection methods Culture methods for coronaviruses are available; however, due to the difficulty of culturing coronaviruses, molecular methods have been more widely used for detec- tion in water (see section 7.4). Source and occurrence Nucleic acids from SARS-CoV-1, SARS-CoV-2 and MERS-CoV have been detected in urine and faeces. Despite widespread detection of SARS-CoV-2 RNA in sewage, there is no evidence that infectious virus is present in faecal wastes and environmen- tal waters or causes infection by this route. The persistence of infectious coronavi- ruses in water is considered to be short to moderate (up to 1 month at 20 °C). Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4 ), control measures to manage potential but unidenti- fied risks from coronaviruses should include application of adequate water treatment processes, and protection of drinking-water quality during storage and distribution. Evidence suggests chlorine would be an effective drinking-water disinfectant to inac- tivate coronaviruses. As coronaviruses are not regarded as being waterborne, indicator organisms are not relevant. Bibliography WHO (2025) Coronaviridae (SARS-CoV-1, SARS-CoV-2, MERS-CoV and common cold coronaviruses). Background document for the WHO Guidelines for drinking-water quality. Geneva, World Health Organization. Enteroviruses Significance in drinking‑water There is moderate evidence linking transmission of enteroviruses with drinking-water based on a limited number of enterovirus outbreaks where unsafe drinking-water sup- plies were identified as risk factors.

294 295 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA General description Enteroviruses are among the smallest known viruses (20–30 nm in diameter), and consist of a single-stranded RNA genome in a non-enveloped icosahedral capsid. There are 12 species of enteroviruses (A to L), which include over 100 serotypes that infect humans. Among these are poliovirus, coxsackievirus and echovirus, which re- tain their old taxonomic designations as common names. Most enterovirus strains are human specific, but some species infect animals other than humans. None of these non-human-specific forms are known to infect humans. Human health effects Enterovirus infection originates in the gastrointestinal tract. It can cause a broad spec- trum of diseases ranging from mild illness characterized by cough, rash and fever to severe effects ranging from neurological illness, including aseptic meningitis, encepha- litis and poliomyelitis, and respiratory illnesses. Aseptic meningitis appears to be the most common severe clinical manifestation associated with enterovirus infections in children and adults, especially in high-income countries. It has been estimated (in- cluding in a 2017 publication) that mortality rates from severe clinical infections can be as high as 10%. The prevalence of asymptomatic infections can be extremely high for enteroviruses. Reinfection with the same virus often results in milder symptoms or subclinical or asymptomatic infection. Epidemiology Enteroviruses are a common but underreported cause of human infections globally. With the exception of poliomyelitis, the disease burden is poorly estimated. Y oung children are at most risk for infections. Enteroviruses exhibit epidemic and endemic patterns of incidence. Seasonally, infections from enteroviruses have tended to oc- cur in summer in countries in the temperate areas of the northern hemisphere and year-round in tropical areas. Worldwide, Enterovirus B, led by Echovirus 30, was the most detected species with Enterovirus C more often detected in Africa, and Enterovi- rus A in Asia. The global prevalence of poliovirus (Enterovirus C) has decreased due to worldwide eradication efforts through vaccination, but wild polioviruses continue to be detected in some parts of Africa and the eastern Mediterranean. Novel entero- viruses (e.g. D68, enterovirus 71) continue to emerge and may become new public health threats. Transmission Enteroviruses are transmitted by the faecal–oral route and by inhalation of airborne viruses. The relative importance of the different modes of transmission varies with the particular enterovirus and environmental settings. The faecal–oral pathway through person-to-person contact predominates in areas with poor sanitary conditions, while transmission through inhalation predominates in higher-income settings. Oral–oral spread by contact with contaminated saliva may be an exposure pathway. Transmis- sion through contaminated fomites and soil is considered important. Waterborne transmission has been confirmed from two recreational water outbreaks. Drinking- water represents a likely source of enterovirus infection based on three outbreaks associated with drinking-water.

296 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA The infective doses have not been determined or vary for most species of entero- viruses, but they may be as low as one infectious particle. Most enteroviruses have incubation periods of 3–10 days on average. Viruses tend to be shed in stools for 10 days to 2 months after exposure. Some immunity is conferred following infection, with symptoms possibly reduced or subclinical post reinfection. Detection methods A standard method using culture and molecular approaches is available for enterovi- ruses (see section 7.4). However, some species are not readily isolated by cell culture methods (e.g. enterovirus 5). Combining cell culture infectivity and molecular meth- ods may improve the detection of infectious enteroviruses. Source and occurrence Enteroviruses are found in a broad range of water and wastewater environments. They have been often detected in drinking-water sources and occasionally in inadequately treated drinking-water. Prevalence is influenced by the presence of human faeces, par- ticularly sewage (untreated or partially treated). Persistence in water is likely to vary among species, but in general can be considered long (over 1 month at 20 °C). Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4 ), control measures to manage potential risks from en- teroviruses should include protection of source waters from contamination by human faecal waste, application of adequate water treatment processes, and protection of drinking-water quality during storage and distribution. Reduction of enteroviruses by drinking-water treatment varies depending on the process. Enteroviruses have low to moderate resistance to disinfection with chlorine, but doses and contact times typically used in drinking-water treatment should provide adequate inactivation. Due to the smaller size of enteroviruses relative to E. coli, resulting in lower removal by treatment processes such as filtration, and their greater environmental persistence, the absence of E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator of their absence in drinking-water. However, the presence of E. coli is a suitable indicator of the possible presence of human enteroviruses (see section 11.6). Bibliography WHO (2025) Enteroviruses. Background document for the WHO Guidelines for drinking- water quality and the WHO Guidelines on sanitation and health. Geneva, World Health Organization. Filoviruses (Ebola and Marburg viruses) Significance in drinking‑water Filoviruses are of low health significance in drinking-water. There is currently no evi- dence linking transmission with drinking-water. Furthermore, evidence suggests that drinking-water is an unlikely route of transmission.

296 297 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA General description Filoviruses are filamentous (50 by 800–1000 nm), and consist of a single-stranded RNA genome in an enveloped nucleocapsid. The Filoviridae family has five gen- era: Cuevavirus (species Lloviu cuevavirus, not causing human disease); Ebolavirus (species Bundibugyo, Reston, Sudan, Tai Forest and Zaire); Marburgvirus (species Marburg Marburgvirus); Striavirus (species Xilang striavirus); and Thamnovirus (species Huangjiao thamnovirus). Hosts are mammals, including humans, bats and non-human primates. Human health effects Ebola and Marburg viruses cause severe haemorrhagic fevers. Initial symptoms are nonspecific, including fever, chills, rash, fatigue, vomiting and diarrhoea, progress- ing to respiratory, renal and hepatic involvement, massive fluid and electrolyte loss through high-volume diarrhoea, multi-organ failure and mucosal haemorrhage. Case fatality rates in outbreaks caused by filoviruses vary, but can be as high as approxi- mately 90% (according to a number of publications including a 2016 report). Asymp- tomatic infections of Ebola virus have been documented. Epidemiology Filovirus disease occurs mostly in sporadic outbreaks, predominantly in Africa, with cases exported to other regions. Transmission within hospitals has been important in outbreaks, and health-care workers are at a demonstrated risk of infection. Marburg virus was identified from two large laboratory outbreaks in Europe associated with transmission from non-human African primates. Transmission Filoviruses are zoonotic, acquired by humans from animal reservoirs, potentially through bushmeat consumption or other contact with infected animal tissues or body fluids. It then spreads from person to person through mucosal surface contact or through broken skin with infected body fluids, particularly blood and other body fluids contaminated with blood. The significance of environmental sources in the po- tential spread of filoviruses is unclear; outbreaks spread through food, water, surfaces or fomites have not been documented. The relative infectivity of filoviruses in humans is considered high. Detection methods Ebola and Marburg viruses can be detected by cell culture, but this should be under - taken only in high-containment laboratories. Antibody and molecular methods are also available (see section 7.4). Source and occurrence Filoviruses have not been detected in drinking-water sources or wastewater, although one study detected Ebola genetic material in wastewater. Faecal contamination of drinking-water sources is not expected since Ebola viruses are not likely to be in fae- ces. Their persistence in water is expected to be short (up to 1 week at 20 °C).

298 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4 ), control measures to manage potential but uniden- tified risks from filoviruses should include application of adequate water treatment processes, and protection of drinking-water quality during storage and distribution. Evidence suggests chlorine would be an effective drinking-water disinfectant to inac- tivate filoviruses. As filoviruses are not regarded as being waterborne, indicator organ- isms are not relevant. Bibliography WHO (2025) Filoviridae (Ebola and Marburg viruses). Background document for the WHO Guidelines for drinking-water quality. Geneva, World Health Organization. Hepatitis A virus Significance in drinking‑water Hepatitis A virus (HAV), also known as Hepatovirus A , is an important waterborne pathogen, with strong evidence from many outbreaks linking transmission to drink- ing-water. A common risk associated with outbreaks is consumption of untreated and vulnerable groundwater. General description HAV consists of a single-stranded RNA genome in a non-enveloped, icosahedral cap- sid that is 27–35 nm in diameter. HAV includes six genotypes with genotypes I–III including sub-genotypes A and B associated with human infection. Genotypes IV–VI are associated with infections in simians. There is no evidence of cross-species trans- mission. Human health effects HAV causes the liver disease hepatitis A, commonly known as infectious hepatitis. Hepatitis A is clinically indistinguishable from other forms of hepatitis. It is charac- terized by a sudden onset of fever, malaise, nausea, anorexia, abdominal discomfort and eventually jaundice (yellowing of the skin and white of the eyes). Itchiness, dark urine and pale stools may also occur. Symptoms of hepatitis A develop, on average, around 4 weeks after infection. In most cases, hepatitis A resolves without treatment, but it can sometimes progress to life-threatening acute liver failure. The severity of illness increases with age and those with pre-existing liver problems. The majority of young children experience asymptomatic infection or mild symptoms, while older children and adults often experience symptomatic disease. Mortality is rare and is higher in those over 40 years of age. Epidemiology The highest rates of acute infections and deaths occur in low- and lower-middle- income countries. In such settings, endemicity is high, and children are often infected at a very early age. In high-income countries, childhood infections are rare, so older children and adults remain susceptible unless vaccinated. Circulation of HAV geno- types and subtypes varies geographically, with genotype I being the most prevalent

298 299 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA worldwide, subgenotype IA being more common than IB, and subgenotype IIIA in- creasingly circulating in some Asian countries and causing outbreaks in Europe. Transmission Transmission is primarily by the faecal–oral route, but can also occur by sexual, (drug) injection or parenteral routes including transfusions. Person-to-person spread is probably the most common route of transmission, but contaminated food and water are important sources of infection. Travel from low to intermediate endemic regions (areas with good sanitation and water supplies) to high endemic areas with- out immunization provides a high risk of infection. HAV is considered to be highly infective, with estimated doses associated with 50% infection rates of tissue culture cells (TCID50) of 10–100. The incubation period for HAV infection is 28–30 days on average. Shedding in faeces can begin several weeks before symptoms occur, reaching its peak concurrently with gastrointestinal symptoms and tapering off as the patient shows symptoms of jaundice. Infection with HAV confers lifelong immunity. Detection methods HAV cannot be readily detected by cell culture, but there are molecular methods (see section 7.4). Combining cell culture infectivity and molecular methods may improve the detection of infectious HAV . Source and occurrence HAV is found in a broad range of water and wastewater environments. It has often been found in surface water and occasionally in groundwater and inadequately treated drinking-water. HAV is reported to be more prevalent in water in low-income coun- tries, in particular, in Africa and the eastern Mediterranean, compared to in high- income countries. Prevalence is influenced by the presence of human faeces includ- ing sewage (untreated or partially treated). HAV has long persistence in water (over 1 month at 20 °C), with survival likely influenced by the composition of other organisms. Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4 ), control measures to reduce potential risk from HAV should include protection of source waters from contamination by human faecal waste, application of adequate water treatment processes, and protection of drinking- water quality during storage and distribution. Reduction of HAV by drinking-water treatment varies depending on the process. HAV is moderately resistant to disinfec- tion with chlorine, but doses and contact times typically used in drinking-water treat- ment should provide adequate inactivation. Due to the smaller size of HAV relative to E. coli, resulting in lower removal by treatment processes such as filtration, and their greater environmental persistence, the absence of E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator of its absence in drinking-water. However, the presence of E. coli is a suitable indicator for the possible presence of HAV (see section 11.6). Bibliography WHO (2025) Hepatitis A virus. Background document for the WHO Guidelines for drinking- water quality and the WHO Guidelines on sanitation and health. Geneva, World Health Organization.

300 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Hepatitis E virus Significance in drinking‑water Hepatitis E virus (HEV) is a significant waterborne pathogen with strong evidence from large outbreaks in low- and middle-income areas linking transmission to drinking-water. These outbreaks occurred in areas with poor sanitation, indicating faecal contamination of drinking-water. General description HEV consists of a single-stranded RNA genome in a non-enveloped icosahedral capsid with a diameter of 27–34 nm. HEV including the strains associated with waterborne disease and previously known as Orthohepevirus A , is now named Paslahepevirus balayani. HEV is subdivided into eight genotypes. Genotypes 1 and 2 have been found only in humans, genotypes 3, 4 and 7 in humans and animal species such as pigs, wild boars, deer, rats and camels, and potential zoonotic transmission of genotypes 5 and 8. Human health effects HEV causes symptoms that are clinically indistinguishable from hepatitis from other causes. Symptoms usually resolve, varying among individuals, but often include an- orexia, jaundice, liver enlargement, abdominal pain, nausea and fever. More severe outcomes associated with HEV infection, especially in high-risk populations (e.g. pre- existing liver disease, transplant patients), include fulminant hepatic failure, a range of neurological syndromes, renal injury, pancreatitis and haematological disorders, but also death. Mortality rates are usually low, but it has been reported (including in a 2023 WHO fact sheet), that they can reach 20–25% in pregnant women infected in the third trimester. There are also higher mortality rates in high-risk populations. Asymptomatic infection is common. Epidemiology HEV has a characteristic distribution. HEV is endemic and causes clinical diseases in low- and middle-income countries, where genotypes 1 and 2 are more prevalent. Outbreaks in such settings have been associated with flooding and monsoon seasons. First infections are typically seen in young adults. Large outbreaks have also occurred in areas of conflict and in displaced populations. Although seroprevalence can be high, clinical cases and outbreaks are rare in higher-income countries. In these settings, no prominent HEV seasonality has been observed, and genotypes 3 and 4 are more com- mon in those over 50 years of age and males are most affected. Transmission Transmission is primarily by the faecal–oral route, with very large waterborne out- breaks involving thousands of cases due to genotypes 1 and 2 documented. Food is an important source of exposure of genotypes 3 and 4. Direct contact with infected animals may also serve as a route of exposure for some genotypes but not genotypes 1 and 2. Person-to-person transmission is not common, but transmission associated with the vertical (mother-to-child) route (particularly genotypes 1 and 2), transfu- sions and organ transplants (particularly genotypes 3 and 4) is possible. The relative infectivity for HEV is unknown, but similar to other enteric viruses, it is expected to be

300 301 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA high (infective doses of 1–10 2 organisms). The average incubation period is 40 days. HEV is excreted in faeces from approximately 1 week before the onset of symptoms and usually persists for 2–4 weeks. Immunity following infection was initially thought to be lifetime, but may wane with time. Detection methods HEV cannot be readily detected by cell culture, but there are molecular methods (see section 7.4). Combining cell culture infectivity and molecular methods may improve the detection of infectious HEV . Source and occurrence There are limited data on the occurrence of HEV , but it has been detected in water and wastewater environments including surface water, groundwater and inadequately treated drinking-water. Prevalence is influenced by the presence of human faeces in- cluding sewage (untreated or partially treated) and possibly animal faecal material. There are no data on the persistence of the virus in water, but similar to other non- enveloped viruses, it is likely to be long (over 1 month at 20 °C). Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4 ), control measures to reduce potential risk from HEV should include protection of source waters from contamination by human and ani- mal faecal wastes, application of adequate water treatment processes, and protec- tion of drinking-water quality during storage and distribution. Reduction of HEV by drinking-water treatment varies depending on the process. HEV has a low to moder- ate resistance to disinfection with chlorine, but doses and contact times typically used in drinking-water treatment should provide adequate inactivation. Due to the smaller size of HEV relative to E. coli, resulting in lower removal by treatment processes such as filtration, and its likely environmental persistence, the absence of E. coli (or ther - motolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator of its absence in drinking-water. However, the presence of E. coli is a suitable indicator for the possible presence of HEV (see section 11.6). Bibliography WHO (2025) Hepatitis E virus. Background document for the WHO Guidelines for drinking- water quality and the WHO Guidelines on sanitation and health. Geneva, World Health Organization. Noroviruses Significance in drinking‑water Noroviruses are major waterborne pathogens, with strong evidence from numerous outbreaks linking transmission to drinking-water. Common risk factors include sew- age contamination and inadequate or failed disinfection. General description Noroviruses (previously known as Norwalk viruses) consist of a single-stranded RNA genome in a non-enveloped icosahedral capsid, and are 30–35 nm in size. There are

302 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA at least seven known norovirus genogroups, GI to GVII, further subdivided into 32 genotypes. Human infection is most commonly caused by viruses belonging to GII, especially genotype 4 (GII.4), as well as GI, and to a very limited extent, GIV . Humans are the only established reservoir for human infective norovirus strains. Human noro- virus genogroups have also been detected in animal hosts, such as mice, cows, dogs and pigs, suggesting a potential for zoonotic transmission. Human health effects Symptoms of norovirus infection typically include an abrupt onset of nausea, vomit- ing (often projectile) and diarrhoea. In healthy individuals, the illness is usually self- limiting, with symptoms lasting for 24–72 hours. Dehydration is the most common complication. Some cases may become severe and require prompt medical treatment. Asymptomatic norovirus prevalence varies depending on settings and countries, but can be common. Asymptomatic individuals may play an important role in norovirus outbreaks. Epidemiology Noroviruses are a frequent cause of diarrhoeal disease, contributing to significant disease burdens in all income settings. Severe cases and deaths have been reported primarily in people over 65 years in high-income countries, and in young children in low- and middle-income countries. Immunocompromised individuals are also more susceptible to infection, with more prolonged and severe symptoms. The majority of reported outbreaks are associated with semi-closed and crowded settings such as long-term health-care facilities, schools, hospitals, child day-care centres, cruise ships and hotels or other lodging facilities. In temperate regions, norovirus infection is a seasonal illness, with the peak of cases and outbreaks occurring in winter months. In tropical climates and in low-income settings, there is some evidence of year-round cir- culation, but patterns are less clear. GII.4 is the predominant outbreak strain globally, with new clusters or variants of the strain emerging every 2–5 years, often resulting in pandemics such as the 2012 pandemic caused by the GII.4 Sydney strain. Since 2012, non-GII.4 strains have emerged and become predominant in several countries. Transmission Noroviruses are transmitted primarily by the faecal–oral route. Person-to-person con- tact is the most important means of transmission, with other sources being contami- nated food, water and fomites. Drinking-water such as tap water, well and spring water have been identified as sources of infection. Vomitus–oral transmission can also occur through aerosolization, followed by ingestion or environmental contamination. The relative infectivity of noroviruses is considered to be high. The dose associ- ated with a 50% infection rate (ID50) is estimated to be as low as 10–20 virus particles. The median incubation period for symptomatic GI and GII infections is estimated to be as low as 1.2 days. Norovirus spreads most easily during the acute stage of disease, and may be shed for 2–3 weeks after symptoms resolve. Asymptomatically infected individuals have also been shown to shed pathogens in similar concentra- tions as symptomatic individuals, although based on studies in health-care settings, asymptomatic individuals do not seem to transmit noroviruses as commonly. Immu-

302 303 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA nity to noroviruses post infection is relatively short, and reinfections are common. A subpopulation of some individuals is resistant to infection by several norovirus genotypes including GII.4. Detection methods Noroviruses are not readily detected by cell culture, but standard molecular methods are available (see section 7.4). Advances in culturing noroviruses in human intestinal enteroids may provide a useful detection method. Combining cell culture infectivity and molecular methods may improve the detection of infectious noroviruses. Source and occurrence Noroviruses are found in a broad range of water and wastewater environments. They have been found often in surface water and occasionally in groundwater and drinking- water. Prevalence is influenced by the presence of human faeces including sewage (untreated or partially treated). Noroviruses can persist for long periods in water (over 1 month at 20 °C). Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4), control measures to reduce potential risk from norovi- ruses should include protection of source waters from contamination by human faecal waste, application of adequate water treatment processes, and protection of drinking- water quality during storage and distribution. Reduction of noroviruses by drinking- water treatment varies depending on the process. Based on studies with non-human noroviruses, it is likely that disinfection processes, including chlorination, will be effec- tive for inactivating human strains of norovirus. Due to the smaller size of noroviruses relative to E. coli, resulting in lower removal by treatment processes such as filtration, and their greater environmental persistence, the absence of E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator of their absence in drinking-water. However, the presence of E. coli is a suitable indicator of the possible presence of noroviruses (see section 11.6). Bibliography WHO (2025) Noroviruses. Background document for the WHO Guidelines for drinking- water quality and the WHO Guidelines on sanitation and health. Geneva, World Health Organization. Orthomyxoviruses (Influenza viruses) Significance in drinking‑water Influenza viruses are of low health significance in drinking-water. There is no evi- dence linking transmission with drinking-water. General description Influenza viruses have a single-stranded RNA genome in an enveloped nucleocap- sid with a diameter of 80–120 nm. The Orthomyxoviridae family has seven genera, three containing species of human health importance: influenza A, influenza B and influenza C viruses. Influenza A viruses infect humans, birds and a range of other

304 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA mammals. Birds and swine are important to human transmission. Influenza B viruses infect mostly humans, and influenza C viruses infect humans, swine and dogs. Viral subtypes are designated by their hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N) types (e.g. H1N1). Influenza B viruses are not divided into subtypes, but two distinct lineages circulate among humans. Human health effects Influenza viruses cause a range of respiratory illnesses in humans, from mild to fatal. Seasonal influenza caused by influenza A and influenza B is characterized by a sudden onset of fever, cough, headache, muscle and joint pain, severe malaise, sore throat and a runny nose. Gastrointestinal symptoms can also occur, particularly in children, but there is no conclusive evidence that these symptoms are due to intestinal infection and they may be due to inflammatory responses in the gut. The prevalence of asymptomatic influenza infections (including based on a 2022 review) can be greater than 50%. Sec- ondary bacterial pneumonia is a frequent complication following influenza infection. Epidemiology The burden of seasonal influenza is substantial. Children, adults greater than 65 years of age, people with chronic illness and immunocompromised people are at higher risk for complicated illness or death. The epidemiology of human influenza viruses can be broadly divided into epidemic and pandemic spread. Epidemics typically occur in annual seasonal cycles that peak in winter months in temperate climates. Influenza can occur throughout the year in tropical regions, causing more irregular outbreaks. Although reported sporadically, the transmission of avian and swine influenza viruses from animals to humans is uncommon. Transmission Seasonal influenza viruses are primarily transmitted by the respiratory route, spread- ing from person to person; droplets and droplet nuclei play a role in transmission. Transmission can also take place by hand-to-mucous membrane contact, which may be either direct hand-to-hand contact or possibly by indirect hand-to-hand contact via surfaces and fomites. Outbreak spread through food or water has not been docu- mented. Zoonotic transmission can be either animal-to-human followed by limited person-to-person transmission, or by re-assortment of animal and human viruses (antigenic shift), producing new strains that subsequently spread from person to per- son. The incubation period is short, usually 1–5 days. The relative infectivity of influ- enza viruses is considered high, although data are limited. Detection methods Influenza viruses can be detected by mammalian cell culture or in embryonated chicken eggs; however, molecular methods have been more widely used for detection in water (see section 7.4). Source and occurrence Influenza viruses or nucleic acids most likely from avian and swine sources have been detected in surface waters, groundwaters or farm waters. Influenza virus nucleic acids

304 305 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA have been detected in surface water during human outbreaks. Prevalence is influ- enced by the presence of faecal waste. Influenza viruses are likely to persist for long periods in surface water (over 1 month at 20 °C). Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4 ), control measures to reduce potential microbial risks should be effective against influenza viruses. These include protection of source waters from contamination by human and animal faecal wastes, application of ad- equate water treatment processes, and protection of drinking-water quality during storage and distribution. Reduction of influenza viruses by drinking-water treat- ment varies depending on the process. Studies of susceptibility of influenza viruses to drinking-water disinfectants are limited, but suggest chlorine is effective in inac- tivating influenza viruses. Due to the smaller size of influenza viruses relative to E. coli, resulting in lower removal by treatment processes such as filtration, and their expected longer environmental persistence, the absence of E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator of their absence in drinking-water. However, the presence of E. coli is a suitable indicator of the possible presence of influenza viruses (see section 11.6). Bibliography WHO (2025) Orthomyxoviridae (Influenza viruses). Parechoviruses Significance in drinking‑water Human parechoviruses (HPeVs) are of low health significance in drinking-water. Although HPeVs can be transmitted by the faecal–oral route and have been detected in sewage and surface water, there is no evidence linking transmission with drinking- water. General description Human parechoviruses (HPeVs) are small (28 nm in diameter), and consist of a single-stranded RNA genome in a non-enveloped capsid. There are four species of Parechovirus: Parechovirus A (formerly named Human Parechovirus), Parechovirus B (formerly named Ljungan virus), Parechovirus C (Sebokele virus) and Parechovirus D (Ferret parechovirus). Parechovirus A consists of 19 types, HPeV-1 to HPeV-19, based on phylogenetic analysis of amino acid sequences of the viral capsid protein. Humans are the only known reservoir for the human disease-causing strains of HPeVs. Human health effects Infection can cause mild to severe illness, with symptoms including diarrhoea and flu- like disease as well as severe diseases such as meningoencephalitis, sepsis and flaccid paralysis. Clinical manifestation of HPeV infection varies between HPeV genotypes. HPeV-3 causes severe disease in neonates and infants younger than 3 months of age. Most individuals infected with HPeVs are asymptomatic.

306 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Epidemiology HPeV infections are globally endemic throughout the year. In temperate climates, HPeV infections peak during the summer and autumn. Biannual cycles of infection have also been observed. Children under 2 years of age are at the greatest risk of devel- oping symptomatic HPeV infection. Transmission Transmission is through the faecal–oral and respiratory routes. HPeVs can be spread by person-to-person contact, airborne transmission, fomites and possibly contami- nated food and water. The infective dose of HPeV is unknown. Detection methods Cell culture and molecular methods are available for HPeVs (see section 7.4). Source and occurrence HPeVs have been commonly detected in surface water. Prevalence is influenced by the presence of human faeces including sewage (untreated or partially treated). There are no data on persistence, but similar to other non-enveloped viruses, it is likely to be long. Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4 ), control measures to reduce potential microbial risks should be effective against HPeVs. These include protection of source waters from contamination by human faecal waste, application of adequate water treatment pro- cesses, and protection of drinking-water quality during storage and distribution. Reduction of HPeVs by drinking-water treatment varies depending on the process. HPeVs are likely to be moderately resistant to disinfection with chlorine, but doses and contact times typically used in drinking-water treatment should provide ade- quate inactivation. Due to the smaller size of HPeVs relative to E. coli, resulting in lower removal by treatment processes such as filtration, and their expected environ- mental persistence, E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator of their absence in drinking-water. However, the presence of E. coli is a suitable indicator of the possible presence of HPeVs (see section 11.6). Bibliography WHO (2025) Parechoviruses. Rotaviruses Significance in drinking‑water Rotaviruses are major waterborne pathogens, with strong evidence from several wa- terborne outbreaks linking transmission to drinking-water. A common risk factor is inadequate disinfection of drinking-water supplies. General description Rotaviruses consist of a double-stranded RNA genome in a non-enveloped icosa- hedral capsid that is 50–65 nm in diameter. This capsid is surrounded by a double-

306 307 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA layered shell, giving the virus the appearance of a wheel – hence the name rotavirus. The diameter of the entire virus is about 100 nm. There are nine species of rotavirus designated A to D and F to J, each of which consists of a number of subgroups. Species A, B, C and H can infect humans, with species A being the most commonly diagnosed cause of rotavirus infections. Rotavirus A is further divided into serotypes using char- acteristics of the outer capsid proteins VP4 and VP7. Several unique types of VP4 (P types) and VP7 (G types) are currently known, demonstrating great antigenic diver - sity. Humans are the only established reservoir for human infective rotavirus strains. There is some evidence that animal rotavirus strains can infect humans, suggesting a potential for zoonotic transmission. Human health effects Acute human rotavirus infection has an abrupt onset of severe watery diarrhoea, with fever, abdominal pain and vomiting. Dehydration and metabolic acidosis may develop, and the outcome may be fatal if the infection is not treated appropriately, especially in infants and underweight children. Adults tend to have similar but milder symptoms compared to children. Infections may also be asymptomatic, especially in older children and adults. Epidemiology The burden of diarrhoeal disease caused by rotavirus among infants and young chil- dren is extremely high, with nearly every child infected by 5 years of age. It is also the cause of a substantial proportion of diarrhoeal disease mortality. Differences in transmission patterns, health-care access, childhood co-infections and co-morbidities drive substantial differences in the rotavirus disease burden between low- and high- income settings The rotavirus disease burden is greater in low-income than in high- income settings, and most rotavirus deaths occur in low-income settings. The relative importance of rotavirus in contributing to diarrhoeal disease is expected to decrease due to the use of rotavirus vaccines. In low-income, typically tropical settings, there is usually a background of year-round circulation punctuated by episodes of intense transmission, but some studies suggest there is some seasonality with peaks during cooler and drier months. In higher-income, temperate regions, illnesses peak in win- ter and spring months. Transmission Human rotaviruses are transmitted primarily by the faecal–oral route. Person-to- person contact is likely the most important source of transmission, with other sources being contaminated food, drinking-water or fomites. Airborne transmission of aero- solized virus is also possible. Rotaviruses are highly infective, with an estimated dose associated 50% infection rate (ID 50) of 6 focus-forming units. The incubation period can range from 24 to 48 hours. Rotaviruses are excreted from 2 days before and up to 10 days after symptomatic illness. Rotavirus reinfections are quite common through- out life, although with each reinfection, the illness tends to become milder. Detection methods Wild-type strains of rotavirus A are not readily detected by cell culture, but there are molecular methods to determine the presence and type of rotavirus (see section 7.4).

MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA A combined cell culture and molecular method has been used to detect infectious rotaviruses. Source and occurrence Rotaviruses are found in a broad range of water and wastewater environments, and have been often found in surface water. Rotaviruses have also been detected in ground- water and drinking-water. Prevalence is influenced by the presence of human faeces including sewage (untreated or partially treated). They can persist for long periods in water (over 1 month at 20 °C). Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4), control measures to reduce potential risk from rotavi- ruses should include protection of source waters from contamination by human faecal waste, application of adequate water treatment processes, and protection of drinking- water quality during storage and distribution. Reduction of rotaviruses by drinking- water treatment varies depending on the process. Rotaviruses are moderately resis- tant to free chlorine, but doses and contact times typically used in drinking-water treatment should provide adequate inactivation. Due to the smaller size of rotaviruses relative to E. coli, resulting in lower removal by treatment processes such as filtration, and their greater environmental persistence, the absence of E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator of their absence in drinking-water. However, the presence of E. coli is a suitable indicator of the possible presence of human rotaviruses (see section 11.6). Bibliography WHO (2025) Rotaviruses. Sapoviruses Significance in drinking‑water There is moderate evidence linking transmission of sapoviruses with drinking-water from a limited number of outbreaks associated with sapoviruses, in conjunction with other pathogens. Risk factors include lack of treatment and sewage contamination through failures in drinking-water distribution systems. General description Sapoviruses consist of a single-stranded RNA genome in a non-enveloped capsid that is 30–38 nm in diameter. Sapoviruses include 19 different genogroups, with viruses infecting humans belonging to genogroups I, II, IV and V . These genogroups are fur- ther subdivided into 19 genotypes: GI and GII each comprise 8 genotypes, GIV has only 1 genotype and GV has 2 genotypes. Humans are the only established reservoir for human infective strains of Sapovirus. Other genogroups have been shown to infect animals such as pigs, mink, dogs, sea lions and bats. Phylogenetic analysis showing that animals have contributed to sapovirus epidemiology suggests a potential for zoo- notic transmission.

308 309 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Human health effects Sapoviruses cause gastrointestinal illness that cannot be clinically distinguished from illness caused by noroviruses. Symptoms are typically mild to moderate, with abrupt onset of primary symptoms including nausea, vomiting (often projectile) and diar - rhoea. Dehydration is the most common complication. In most cases, symptoms re- solve within 1 week. Deaths from Sapovirus infections are rare, but have been reported in elderly patients. A number of small-scale studies suggest there is also a high level of asymptomatic carriage among healthy individuals. Epidemiology Sapoviruses affect people of all ages worldwide, but sporadic cases occur more fre- quently in young children. Outbreaks are most common among elderly people living in long-term care facilities, and children at day-care centres. Research into other sus- ceptible groups such as immunocompromised individuals is scarce, but such groups may be at higher risk of severe infection and prolonged viral shedding. Sapovirus infections show a marked seasonality in temperate climates, with increased activity usually peaking in colder months. Transmission Sapoviruses are transmitted primarily by the faecal–oral route. Person-to-person con- tact is the most important means of transmission, with other sources being contami- nated food and fomites and possibly water. Vomitus–oral transmission can also occur through aerosolization, followed by ingestion or environmental contamination. The relative infectivity of sapoviruses is unknown, but similar to other enteric viruses, it is likely to be high (infective doses of 1–10 2 organisms). The average incu- bation period for symptomatic infection is 1.7 days with viral shedding decreasing gradually after the onset of symptoms. Reinfection and recurrence of illness can occur, suggesting that immunity is genotype specific, with little cross-protection even within genogroups. Detection methods Cell culture methods for detecting sapoviruses are not available, but molecular meth- ods are available (see section 7.4). Combining cell culture infectivity and molecular methods may improve the detection of infectious sapoviruses. Source and occurrence Sapoviruses are found in a broad range of water and wastewater environments. However, there are limited data on the presence of sapoviruses in surface water and drinking-water. They have not been detected in groundwater, although data are lim- ited. There are no data on persistence of sapoviruses, but it is likely to be similar to noroviruses, which can persist for long periods in water (over 1 month at 20 °C). Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4), control measures to reduce potential risk from sapovi- ruses should include protection of source waters from contamination by human faecal waste, application of adequate water treatment processes, and protection of drinking-

310 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA water quality during storage and distribution. Reduction of sapoviruses by drinking- water treatment varies depending on the process. Similar to noroviruses, it is likely that disinfection processes, including chlorination will be effective for inactivating sapoviruses. Due to the smaller size of sapoviruses relative to E.coli, resulting in lower removal by treatment processes such as filtration, and their likely environmental per- sistence, the absence of E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator of their absence in drinking-water. However, the presence of E. coli is a suitable indi- cator of the potential presence of human sapoviruses (see section 11.6). Bibliography WHO (2025) Sapoviruses. Geneva, World Health Organization. 11.3 Protozoan pathogens Most pathogenic protozoa with moderate to strong evidence of waterborne transmis- sion are enteric pathogens. Cryptosporidium , Giardia and Toxoplasma are zoonotic with important animal sources. In the case of Toxoplasma , humans are intermediate hosts with infection not leading to excretion of oocysts. There are also two free-living protozoa – Naegleria fowleri and Acanthamoeba – that can grow in water environ- ments, including in biofilms in drinking-water distribution systems. Enteric protozoa are transmitted by ingestion of contaminated drinking-water, while Acanthamoeba is transmitted primarily by contact where contaminated drinking-water is used for cleaning or storing contact lenses and N. fowleri when contaminated water enters nasal passages. For further information, including an overview of treatment consider- ations for protozoa, see section 7.2.2. Acanthamoeba Significance in drinking‑water Acanthamoeba are not transmitted through the ingestion of drinking-water. However, there is strong evidence for water-based transmission of Acanthamoeba leading to eye infections through the use of non-sterile water including drinking-water to clean or store contact lenses. In addition, Acanthamoeba can harbour bacterial pathogens such as Legionella and potentially enteric viruses, and may play a role in their survival and the pathogenicity of Legionella in drinking-water. General description Acanthamoeba are free-living amoebae commonly found in fresh water and soil. Their life cycle includes two stages: an actively growing trophozoite (12–35 µm) and a dor - mant cyst (5–20 µm) that forms and survives in response to adverse environmental conditions. There are over 20 species of Acanthamoeba. Historically, they were catego- rized into three groups based on size and cyst morphology. More recently, Acantham- oeba have been divided into 20 genotypes based on DNA sequencing. Genotype T4, which includes A. castellani, is the most common disease-causing genotype.

310 311 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Human health effects Acanthamoeba infections are commonly asymptomatic, but Acanthamoeba can cause three types of disease. In immunocompetent people, the most common disease is an eye infection known as acanthamoebic keratitis (AK). Symptoms of AK include inflammation of the cornea, blurred vision, ulceration and blindness. Infections of the central nervous system known as granulomatous amoebic encephalitis (GAE) and cutaneous (skin) infections can occur in immune-deficient individuals. Clinical symptoms of GAE are similar to meningitis and include headache, fever, lethargy, stiff neck, confusion and irritability. GAE can lead to death in some instances. The lack of distinguishing features of GAE makes diagnosis difficult. Symptoms of cutaneous infections include skin lesions and nodules, or sinus lesions and sinusitis. Epidemiology Although there is no global estimate for AK, it is likely widespread due to the com- mon and increasing use of contact lenses and the ubiquity of Acanthamoeba in the environment. The majority of cases of AK occur in wearers of soft contact lenses. GAE and cutaneous infection are predominantly identified in immunocompromised or debilitated individuals and are extremely rare in immunocompetent people. Transmission The most common route of transmission for AK in wearers of contact lenses is the use of contaminated water for washing or storing contact lenses. Swimming, using a spa or showering while wearing contact lenses also present a risk of infection. Infections can also occur following eye injury or surgery. Ingestion of drinking-water is not a route of transmission. Person-to-person and zoonotic transmissions of Acantham - oeba have not been reported. GAE and cutaneous infections are not considered to be waterborne. It is likely that Acanthamoeba enter the bloodstream from other sites of colonization such as the nose, lungs or skin lesions following injury or trauma. The human infective doses associated with any forms of disease caused by Acanthamoeba are unknown. The incubation period for AK is unknown, but is considered to be several days. Detection methods Acanthamoeba can be detected using culture-based methods and subsequently classi- fied using molecular methods (see section 7.4). Source and occurrence Acanthamoeba are very common soil and water organisms. They have been detected in drinking-water supplies, swimming pools, bottled water, seawater and fresh water. Acanthamoeba trophozoites can multiply in water and soil; cysts can form and per - sist for long periods (over 1 month at 20 °C). Acanthamoeba can survive and grow in biofilms in drinking-water distribution systems, including premise plumbing. Prevention and management The most effective control measure to remove the risk of AK arising from drinking- water is to prevent exposure. Drinking-water should not be used for cleaning or storing contact lenses. Within a WSP (see chapter 4), control measures to manage

312 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA potential risks from Acanthamoeba should include application of adequate water treatment processes, protection of drinking-water quality during storage and distri- bution, and minimizing their growth in biofilms in distribution systems and building water systems. Filtration systems designed to remove other protozoa such as Cryp - tosporidium are likely to be effective in removing the larger Acanthamoeba cysts and trophozoites. Acanthamoeba trophozoites are moderately resistant to oxidizing disin- fectants such as chlorine, but doses and contact times typically used in drinking-water treatment should provide adequate inactivation. Cysts are highly resistant to chlorine and relatively resistant to UV light. As Acanthamoeba are non-faecal, environmental organisms that can survive and grow in water, E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator for their possible presence or absence in drinking-water (see section 11.6).
