Balantioides coli Significance in drinking‑water Balantoides coli is of low health significance in drinking-water. Although B. coli is transmitted by the faecal–oral route and has been detected in drinking-water, the evidence linking transmission with drinking-water is weak. Only one waterborne out- break has been reported, occurring in 1971. General description B. coli is a protozoan parasite. It exists in two forms: trophozoites of about 50 mm by 150 mm that are covered with cilia for motility, and environmentally stable cysts of ap- proximately 40–70 mm. Following ingestion of cysts, excystation occurs in the small intestine and the trophozoites colonize the large intestine, where they replicate and form new cysts that are excreted in the faeces. It is the only ciliate that infects humans. Human health effects Human infections of B. coli are relatively rare and most are asymptomatic, but gas- trointestinal illness can occur. Trophozoites can destroy host cells as they multiply. Clinical symptoms may include diarrhoea, nausea, vomiting, headache and anorexia. Illness is typically limited to several days with complete recovery, but some illnesses develop into chronic infections with long duration. Infrequently, and especially in im- munosuppressed hosts or those with other health conditions, illness may progress to dysentery, with possible further spread to other organs. Epidemiology B. coli infection and illness in humans occurs worldwide, with higher rates in immu- nocompromised individuals. Global prevalence was estimated (in a 2017 review) to be about 1%, but could have been as high as 30% in tropical regions where there was high occupational exposures to pigs, especially where sanitation and hygiene were inadequate.

312 313 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Transmission B. coli transmission is by the faecal–oral route, from contact with infections persons or animals, primarily swine or by consumption of contaminated water or food. The only reported waterborne outbreak of balantidiasis occurred from ingestion of water contaminated with swine faeces after a typhoon. Infectivity in humans is unknown. Detection methods Microscopic and molecular methods are available for B. coli. Using microscopy, there is a possibility of confusion with other ciliates of the Balantidium genus that could be present in the water sample. Source and occurrence There are limited data on the occurrence of B. coli cysts, but they have been detected in water and wastewater environments including surface water and inadequately man- aged drinking-water. Prevalence is influenced by the presence of faecal material from humans including sewage (untreated or partially treated) and other animals, particu- larly pigs. B. coli can persist in water for long periods (over 1 month at 20 °C). Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4 ), control measures to reduce potential microbial risks should be effective against B. coli . These include protection of source water from contamination by human and animal faecal wastes, application of adequate water treatment processes, and protection of drinking-water quality during storage and dis- tribution. B. coli cysts are likely removed by conventional filtration methods because of their relatively large size (larger than Cryptosporidium oocysts). Based on data available for other protozoa, they are likely highly resistant to chlorine. Due to the environmen- tal persistence of B. coli cysts and their probable resistance to chemical disinfectants, the absence of E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator of their absence in drinking-water. However, the presence of E. coli is a suitable indicator of the possible presence of B. coli. Bibliography WHO (2025) Balantioides coli. Background document for the WHO Guidelines for drinking- water quality. Geneva, World Health Organization. Blastocystis Significance in drinking‑water Blastocystis is of low health significance in drinking-water. Although Blastocystis is transmitted by the faecal–oral route and has been detected in drinking-water, the evi- dence linking transmission with drinking-water is weak. In addition, there is uncer - tainty about the pathogenicity of Blastocystis. General description Blastocystis are protozoan parasites known since the early 1900s, but knowledge gaps remain about their human pathogenicity. There are at least 17 different subtypes, of which 10 are zoonotic. Subtypes 1–4 are the most common subtypes reported in

314 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA humans. The parasite varies in size between 2 and 40 µm and lives in the host colon in several morphological forms, including the infectious and environmentally resis- tant faecal cyst. Human health effects Blastocystis pathogenicity remains controversial due to nonspecific symptoms and the prevalence of asymptomatic infections. Symptoms include watery or loose stools, di- arrhoea, flatulence, nausea, abdominal pain, anal itching and weight loss. Infections can last for weeks, months or years. In some patients, symptoms resolve, even when Blastocystis remain detectable in stools. In children, Blastocystis infection has been associated with reduced growth outcomes, including stunting, wasting and under - weight status. Epidemiology Blastocystis infections occur globally, and prevalence differs geographically, seasonally and demographically. Prevalence is higher in areas where sanitary and hygienic con- ditions are inadequate and the climate is warm and humid, such as tropical areas with inadequate safe drinking-water, sanitation and hygiene. Blastocystis may be commen- sal organisms that become pathogenic with host changes (e.g. immunosuppression, malnourishment and other infections), although infection occurs in immunocompe- tent and immunocompromised individuals. Infection appears to be widespread among both adults and children, but some studies report peak infections occur between 10 and 14 years of age. Transmission Transmission is mainly faecal–oral, with humans and other animal hosts including insects, reptiles, birds, livestock, domestic pets, rodents and non-human primates all being natural reservoirs for the organism. There is some evidence for transmission from water and food, with not washing hands after toileting, drinking faecally con- taminated water and repeatedly eating outside identified as risk factors. Other risk factors that have been identified include exposure to infected animals and crowded settings such as child-care facilities and schools. Direct contact with infected hu- mans or fomites have also been suggested as exposure sources. The infectious dose is unknown. Detection methods Culture-based methods, in vitro infectivity and molecular methods are available for Blastocystis. Source and occurrence Blastocystis cysts have been detected in water and wastewater environments includ- ing surface water, vulnerable groundwater and inadequately treated drinking-water during investigations of illness associated with water. Prevalence is influenced by the presence of faecal material from humans including sewage (untreated or partially treated) and other animals. Blastocystis cysts can persist in water for long periods (over 1 month at 20 °C).

314 315 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4 ), control measures to reduce potential microbial risks should be effective against Blastocystis. These include protection of source water from contamination by human and animal faecal wastes, application of adequate water treatment processes, and protection of drinking-water quality during storage and distribution. Blastocystis cysts are likely removed by conventional filtration methods because of their size (similar or larger than Cryptosporidium oocysts). They have rela- tively high resistance to chlorine and ozone, but can be inactivated by UV light. Due to the environmental persistence of Blastocystis and their high resistance to chemical disinfectants, E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator of its absence in drinking-water. However, the presence of E. coli is a suitable indicator of the possible presence of Blastocystis. Bibliography WHO (2025) Blastocystis. Background document for the WHO Guidelines for drinking-water quality. Geneva, World Health Organization. Cryptosporidium Significance in drinking‑water Cryptosporidium are major zoonotic waterborne pathogens with strong evidence of transmission through drinking-water from a large number of outbreaks, including those where sewage or livestock faeces were the source of contamination. Outbreaks of cryptosporidiosis are commonly associated with insufficient treatment or treatment malfunction, recent rainfall in water catchments, untreated and vulnerable ground- water sources, and distribution system deficiencies. General description Cryptosporidium are coccidian protozoan parasites with a complex life cycle including sexual and asexual reproduction. Thick-walled Cryptosporidium oocysts found in the environment are typically 4–6 µm. When ingested, the oocysts excyst and complete their life cycle in the small intestine, resulting in production of thin- and thick-walled oocysts. Thin-walled oocysts can excyst within the same host and start a new life cy- cle leading to heavy infections, while thick-walled oocysts are excreted in faeces. Of the 44 Cryptosporidium species, 19 have been reported in humans worldwide, with C. hominis and C. parvum the most frequently reported. Human health effects Cryptosporidium infection (cryptosporidiosis) can result in watery diarrhoea of sudden onset, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and low-grade fever. Asymptom- atic infection can also occur. Symptoms are usually self-limiting and last for up to 2 weeks, but can lead to profound weight loss, prostration, and increased morbidity and mortality. Cryptosporidiosis in malnourished children under 2 years of age has been associated with moderate to severe diarrhoea that can be persistent and result in growth faltering, cognitive deficit disorders and mortality. Severely immunocompro- mised individuals may suffer chronic, severe diarrhoea with significant loss of fluid,

316 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA as infections spread throughout the gastrointestinal tract or to other sites. Seronega- tive reactive arthritis has been reported in adults and children. There is no effective therapy or vaccine for cryptosporidiosis. Epidemiology Cryptosporidiosis is a very common gastrointestinal disease. It is one of the most im- portant causes of diarrhoeal disease and deaths among young children, especially in low-income settings. While both C. hominis and C. parvum cause disease worldwide, there are geographical and seasonal differences with C. hominis dominant in most regions, but C. parvum is more common in selected countries or regions such as the Middle East and New Zealand. There are also differences in distribution between urban and rural areas, with C. hominis more common in urban areas and C. parvum more common in rural areas. In addition to young children, caregivers of infected individuals, travellers to countries where infection is endemic and individuals who handle infected livestock are more likely to become infected. Transmission Cryptosporidium are transmitted by the faecal–oral route. Outbreaks have been re- ported after ingestion of contaminated drinking-water, recreational waters and food, and after contact with infected humans and animals. Livestock (predominantly calves and lambs) are important sources of human infectious C. parvum. The relative infectivities of C. hominis and C. parvum are considered to be high. For C. hominis, the dose associated with a 50% infection rate (ID 50) is estimated at 83 oocysts, while for C. parvum, the ID50 values differ between isolates, ranging from 12 to 455 oocysts. The incubation period is typically 5–7 days. Symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals can shed infective oocysts for weeks to months after infec- tion. While previous infections do not confer immunity, they may protect against diarrhoea and severe disease. Detection methods Standard methods for Cryptosporidium based on microscopy are available, but can- not determine the viability or infectivity of oocysts. Cell cultures and animal models can be used to determine infectivity. Molecular methods are also available to identify C. hominis, C. parvum and other Cryptosporidium species (see section 7.4). Source and occurrence Cryptosporidium oocysts are found in a broad range of water and wastewater envi- ronments. Cryptosporidium have been frequently detected in vulnerable groundwater and inadequately treated drinking-water, with prevalence influenced by rainfall and the presence of faecal material including from human sewage (untreated or partially treated) and animals, particularly cattle. Infective Cryptosporidium oocysts can persist for long periods in water (over 1 month at 20 °C). Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4), control measures to manage potential risks from Cryp- tosporidium oocysts should include protection of source waters from contamination

Filtration processes are important barriers for Cryptosporidium in drinking-water treatment. Cryptosporidium oocysts are highly resistant to chlorine, but UV light and ozone are effective. Due to the environmental persistence of Cryptosporidium oocysts and their resistance to some chemical disin- fectants, the absence of E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator of their absence in drinking-water. However, the presence of E. coli is a suitable indi- cator of the possible presence of Cryptosporidium (see section 11.6). Bibliography WHO (2025) Cryptosporidium. Cyclospora cayetanensis Significance in drinking‑water There is moderate evidence linking transmission of Cyclospora cayetanensis with drinking-water, based on a small number of outbreaks possibly associated with undis- infected or inadequately disinfected drinking-water supplies. General description Cyclospora are coccidian protozoan parasites with a complex life cycle including sexual and asexual reproduction. Environmentally stable oocysts typically measure 8–10 µm. When ingested, the oocysts excyst and complete their life cycle in the small intestine, leading to production of immature oocysts. Once excreted, immature oo- cysts must undergo sporulation over days to weeks to mature infectious oocysts. Nineteen species of Cyclospora have been described, of which C. cayetanensis is the only species in the genus known to infect humans. Human health effects Infection by C. cayetanensis (cyclosporiasis) is characterized by watery diarrhoea, ab- dominal cramping, weight loss, anorexia, myalgia, fatigue, and occasionally vomiting and fever. Serious sequelae such as Guillain–Barré syndrome and Reiter’s syndrome have been reported. Symptoms are usually self-limiting, but relapsing illness can last weeks or months. Increased susceptibility, prolonged diarrhoea, high rates of reoccur- rence and severe intestinal injury have been observed in immunocompromised indi- viduals. Asymptomatic infection is common in endemic areas. Early and persistent exposure is associated with decreased likelihood of symptomatic infection. Treatment is generally not required, but antibiotics can be used to manage cyclosporiasis. Epidemiology C. cayetanensis has a global distribution with predominance in low-income, tropi- cal and subtropical countries where it is often endemic. Community-based studies in endemic settings (included in a 2019 review) have found widely varying infection prevalence rates ranging from 5% to 40%. Children frequently have the highest preva-

318 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA lence rates, although the age range of increased prevalence (e.g. 2–4 years or older) has varied among studies. The moderate to severe childhood diarrhoeal disease burden attributable to C. cayetanensis in low-income, high-burden settings is low compared to other gastrointestinal pathogens. However, attribution in endemic settings is often complicated by the high proportion of asymptomatic cases. In endemic countries, the prevalence of C. cayetanensis has a marked seasonality, but this varies, with prevalence high in some countries during wet seasons and in dry seasons in other countries. This suggests that the life cycle of C. cayetanensis in the environment is likely to be influ- enced by a mixture of factors, such as rainfall, temperature and humidity. In non- endemic settings, infections are observed in the general population regardless of age and immune status, and are almost always symptomatic. Illness is linked mostly to travel to endemic areas or consumption of food from endemic areas. Transmission C. cayetanensis is transmitted by the faecal–oral route. Contaminated food, particu- larly raw fruit and vegetables, appears to be the primary source of transmission in low-income countries. Contact with surface and recreational waters and soils have also been documented as sources. In addition, there is some evidence that ingestion of contaminated water may be a source of exposure. Person-to-person transmission is virtually impossible because oocysts excreted in faeces require a maturation period in the environment in order to sporulate and become infective. Humans are the only confirmed reservoir for C. cayetanensis. The relative infectivity of C. cayetanensis is unknown, but based on the high in- fectivity of oocysts of similar enteric protozoa (e.g. Cryptosporidium ), it is probably high (infective doses of 1–10 2 organisms). The incubation period for cyclosporiasis is typically 1 week. Shedding can be intermittent and can also occur when the host is asymptomatic or for many weeks after symptoms resolve in untreated patients. Although the likelihood of diarrhoeal symptoms decreases with each subsequent in- fection, outbreaks have been reported in endemic areas, which could suggest that any acquired immunity is not long lasting. Detection methods Microscopic and molecular methods are available for Cyclospora oocysts (see sec - tion 7.4). Source and occurrence There are limited data on occurrence, but C. cayetanensis oocysts have been detected in water and wastewater environments including surface water, groundwater and in- adequately treated drinking-water. Prevalence is influenced by faecal contamination from humans including from sewage (untreated or partially treated). They can persist in water for long periods (over 1 month at 20 °C). Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4), control measures to manage potential risks from C. cay- etanensis should include protection of source waters from contamination by human faecal waste (including extra vigilance during heavy rain), application of adequate

318 319 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA water treatment processes, and protection of drinking-water quality during storage and distribution. Filtration processes that are effective against Crytosporidium oocysts should be effective at removing the slightly larger Cyclospora oocysts. Based on their cell wall structure, Cyclospora oocysts are probably highly resistant to chlorine and are expected to be as sensitive to UV light as other protozoan cysts and oocysts. Due to the environmental persistence of Cyclospora oocysts and their probable resistance to chemical disinfectants, the absence of E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator of their absence in drinking-water. However, the presence of E. coli is a suitable indicator of the possible presence of C. cayetanensis (see section 11.6). Bibliography WHO (2025) Cyclospora cayetanensis. Cytoisospora belli Significance in drinking‑water Cytoisospora belli is of low health significance in drinking-water. The evidence linking transmission of C. belli with drinking-water is weak. Although three waterborne out- breaks have been identified, none were epidemiologically associated with drinking- water, but rather with consumption of vegetables irrigated with water from a sewage treatment plant. General description C. belli is a coccidian protozoan parasite. There are many species of Cytoisospora that infect animals, but only C. belli infects humans. C. belli has a complex life cycle includ- ing asexual and sexual replication. Environmentally stable oocysts typically measure 25–35 µm by 18–20 µm. When ingested, the oocysts excyst and complete their life cycle in the small intestine, leading to production of immature oocysts. Once ex- creted in faeces, immature oocysts require a period of 1–2 days in the environment to mature into infectious oocysts. Human health effects Infection can be symptomatic or asymptomatic. Symptoms include a low-grade fe- ver, lassitude and malaise, followed soon by mild, watery diarrhoea, abdominal pain, cramp and nausea. Eosinophilia is a distinctive feature of this pathogen and is not caused by other coccidian parasites. The infection is usually self-limiting and lasts 1–4 weeks. Immunocompromised individuals experience more severe symptoms in which diarrhoea may become intense and prolonged, and lead to weight loss and malabsorp- tion. In rare cases, they may also develop extra-intestinal disease that may spread. Epidemiology Infections with C. belli are widespread in humans, with higher prevalence of infec- tion in immunocompromised people and children. Infections are more common in the tropics and subtropics, although they may occur elsewhere, including in high- income countries. Prevalence also depends on sanitation and hygiene conditions.

320 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA The burden of disease from C. belli is variable, and it is poorly quantified on a global basis. Outbreaks have been reported, especially among immunocompromised hosts and in child-care and health-care facilities where hygiene and sanitation conditions are inadequate. Transmission C. belli is transmitted via the faecal–oral route. Therefore, contaminated water, food and fomites are considered likely sources of transmission. However, transmission from fomites and drinking-water has not been confirmed. Direct person-to-person transmission is unlikely. The infectious dose is unknown. Detection methods C. belli oocysts can be detected by light microscopy. Molecular methods are also avail- able (see section 7.4). Source and occurrence There are limited data on the occurrence of C. belli oocysts, but they have been de- tected in water and wastewater environments including surface waters and inade- quately treated drinking-water, with prevalence influenced by faecal contamination from humans including sewage (untreated or partially treated). The persistence of C. belli is expected to be long (over 1 month at 20 °C), based on studies with other coccidian parasites. Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4 ), control measures to reduce potential microbial risks should be effective against C. belli. These include protection of source water from contamination by human faecal wastes, application of adequate water treatment processes, and protection of drinking-water quality during storage and distribution. C. belli oocysts are likely removed by conventional filtration methods because of their relatively large size (larger than Cryptosporidium oocysts). Based on data available for other protozoa, they are likely to be resistant to chlorine. Due to the likely envi- ronmental persistence of C. belli oocysts and their probable resistance to chemical disinfectants, E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator of their absence in drinking-water. However, the presence of E. coli is a suitable indicator of the possible presence of C. belli. Bibliography WHO (2025) Cytoisospora belli. Entamoeba histolytica Significance in drinking‑water Entamoeba histolytica is a significant waterborne pathogen, with strong evidence from several outbreaks linking transmission to drinking-water. A common risk factor as- sociated with outbreaks is contamination of drinking-water by sewage.

320 321 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA General description Entamoeba are protozoan parasites. Entamoeba cysts found in the environment are typically 10–20 µm. Following ingestion, excystation occurs in the intestine to become feeding, replicative trophozoites (10–50 µm). Some trophozoites may invade human cells throughout the body, while others will develop into cysts that are excreted in the faeces. There are many species of Entamoeba, of which four (E. histolytica, E. polecki, E. coli and E. hartmanni ) are considered human pathogens. The majority of symp- tomatic disease in humans is caused by E. histolytica . Humans are the only known reservoir of E. histolytica. Human health effects There are two main forms of human disease due to E. histolytica: acute intestinal inva- sive amoebiasis and extra-intestinal invasive amoebiasis. Infection can be asymptom- atic or range from mild to life-threatening colitis. Most symptomatic cases present as amoebic dysentery. Symptom onset is gradual, with diarrhoea initially being watery but then becoming mucoid and bloody. Severe abdominal pain is common. Invasive amoebiasis may then progress to ulcerative colitis and perforation of the intestine. Intestinal perforation is the most common cause of death. In uncomplicated cases, recovery from intestinal amoebiasis usually takes several weeks, but in some cases, illness lasts longer. Amoebic liver abscesses are the most common form of extra- intestinal amoebiasis. In rare cases, E. histolytica may invade other parts of the body. The main clinical symptoms are the abrupt onset of pain and local tenderness over the liver. Diarrhoea is usually not present. Several drugs are available to treat amoe- biasis; the choice depends on the disease manifestations. Epidemiology Amoebiasis occurs worldwide, with higher incidence in tropical and subtropical re- gions. Within these regions, there is substantial variation in the prevalence and type of infection, which could be influenced by gender, type of work, ecological and physi- ological factors. Amoebic liver abscesses mainly affect men between the ages of 18 and 50 years. E. histolytica gastrointestinal infection affects all ages, but young children in low-income settings are particularly susceptible. Transmission E. histolytica is transmitted primarily by the faecal–oral route. Person-to-person con- tact and ingestion of faecally contaminated food or water appear to be the most signifi- cant sources of transmission. Sexual transmission through anal–oral contact has also been documented. Risk of transmission is greatest in areas with inadequate sanitation and poor drinking-water quality and crowded living conditions. The relative infectivity of E. histolytica cysts is unknown, but based on the high infectivity of cysts of other similar enteric protozoa (e.g. Giardia duodenalis), it is also assumed to be high (infective doses of 1–10 2 organisms). The incubation period for acute intestinal amoebiasis is typically 2–4 weeks. Pathogen shedding can be months or years, and is usually through asymptomatic carriers and those with chronic infec- tions. Immunity to amoebiasis can develop after infection, but may be short lived.

322 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Detection methods Methods used for E. histolytica detection include microscopy, serology, molecular analysis, antigen detection and amoeba culture with isoenzyme analysis. Molecular methods can also be used for the speciation of Entamoeba (see section 7.4). Source and occurrence There have been limited studies on occurrence of E. histolytica , but it has been de- tected in water and wastewater environments including surface water, groundwater and inadequately treated drinking-water. Prevalence is influenced by faecal contami- nation from humans including sewage (untreated or partially treated). The persis- tence of E. histolytica cysts in water is unknown, but based on the persistence of similar enteric protozoan cysts (e.g. Giardia duodenalis), it is expected to be moderate to long (at least 1 week at 20 °C). Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4 ), control measures to manage potential risks from E. histolytica should include prevention of source water contamination by human faecal waste (including extra vigilance during heavy rain), application of adequate water treatment processes, and protection of drinking-water quality during storage and distribution. Filtration is an effective barrier to E. histolytica cysts, which are larger than Cryptosporidium oocysts. Although E. histolytica cysts are moderately resistant to chlorine, doses and contact times typically used in drinking-water treat- ment should provide adequate inactivation. E. histolytica cysts are expected to be as sensitive to UV light as other protozoan cysts and oocysts. Due to the probably long environmental persistence of E. histolytica cysts and their moderate resistance to chemical disinfectants, the absence of E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator of its absence in drinking-water. However, the presence of E. coli is a suitable indicator of the possible presence of E. histolytica (see section 11.6). Bibliography WHO (2025) Entamoeba histolytica. Giardia duodenalis Significance in drinking‑water Giardia duodenalis is a significant zoonotic waterborne pathogen, with strong evidence from a large number of outbreaks linking transmission to drinking-water. Outbreaks of Giardia infection are commonly associated with insufficient treatment or treatment malfunction, untreated and vulnerable groundwater sources, and distribution system deficiencies. General description G. duodenalis (synonyms G. lamblia and G. intestinalis ) are motile, protozoan para- sites. G. duodenalis are separated into eight genetic assemblages (A to H) that have dif-

322 323 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA ferent hosts. Assemblages A and B are found in humans and other primates, cats, dogs and some wild mammals, and are generally regarded as zoonotic. Assemblage A is also prevalent in livestock. Other assemblages are not pathogenic to humans. Giardia cysts found in the environment measure 11–14 µm by 7–10 µm. Following ingestion, excys- tation occurs to become trophozoites, which replicate in the duodenum. Further down the intestinal tract, trophozoites develop into cysts, which are excreted in the faeces. Human health effects Giardia infection (giardiasis) can result in a watery diarrhoea that comes with a broad spectrum of gastrointestinal symptoms, including flatulence, bloating, weight loss, ab- dominal cramping, nausea, malabsorption, greasy and foul-smelling stools, fatigue and chills. These symptoms may last for weeks, and can be chronic and recurring. Failure to thrive can occur, particularly in young children, with weight loss. Asymptomatic infections can occur, especially in children, in highly endemic areas and in persons with prior infections. Giardiasis is often regarded as a benign gastrointestinal illness, although chronic or debilitating giardiasis has been reported. Giardiasis is usually a self-limiting infection, but anti-parasitic drugs can be used to treat serious, chronic or recurring infections. Epidemiology Giardiasis is a very common intestinal infection worldwide. Giardiasis is most fre- quently seen in young children in both low- and high-income countries. Others more likely to become infected include caregivers of infected individuals and travellers to countries where infection is endemic. The current understanding of giardiasis is lim- ited by the lack of monitoring and reporting systems in many countries. Transmission G. duodenalis is transmitted by the faecal–oral route. Transmission occurs frequently in environments where personal hygiene levels are challenged, such as child day-care centres or in disadvantaged communities. Most giardiasis cases occur sporadically, but common source outbreaks can occur. Transmission sources for giardiasis include water, food, and person-to-person and animal contact. Most waterborne outbreaks are associated with drinking-water and recreational water. The relative infectivity of G. duodenalis is considered high. The dose associated with a 50% infection rate (ID 50) for G. duodenalis was calculated at 35 cysts from a series of challenge studies in adult males. The incubation period ranges from 3 days post infection to up to 3 weeks, depending upon the assemblage, dose and host factors such as immune status. Cysts are infectious for as long as they are being excreted. Two studies of waterborne outbreaks suggested that previous infection with Giardia may produce some level of protection against reinfection. Detection methods Standard methods for Giardia based on light microscopy are available, but cannot determine the viability or infectivity of oocysts. Molecular methods are available to identify Giardia species and subtypes including assemblages A and B (see section 7.4).

324 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Source and occurrence Giardia cysts are found in a broad range of water and wastewater environments. Giardia have been frequently detected in surface water and have been detected in vulnerable groundwater and inadequately treated drinking-water. Prevalence is influ- enced by rainfall and the presence of faecal material, including from human sewage (untreated or partially treated) and animals. Giardia cysts can persist for moderate to long periods in water (1 week to over 1 month at 20 °C), with survival influenced by temperature and other environmental factors. Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4), control measures to manage potential risk from Giardia should include protection of source waters from contamination by animal and human faecal wastes (including extra vigilance during heavy rain), application of adequate water treatment processes, and protection of drinking-water quality during storage and distribution. Filtration processes are important barriers for Giardia in drinking- water treatment. Although Giardia cysts are highly resistant to chlorine, it can be ef- fective where drinking-water storage facilities provide adequate contact times. Giardia cysts are sensitive to UV light. Due to the environmental persistence of Giardia cysts and their resistance to chemical disinfectants, the absence of E. coli (or thermotoler - ant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator of the absence of G. duodenalis in drinking- water. However, the presence of E. coli is a suitable indicator of the possible presence of G. duodenalis (see section 11.6). Bibliography WHO (2025) Giardia duodenalis. Microsporidia Significance in drinking‑water Microsporidia are of low health significance in drinking-water. Although microspo- ridia are transmitted by the faecal–oral route and have been detected in drinking- water, the evidence linking transmission with drinking-water is weak. Epidemiologi- cal evidence from a single outbreak is inconclusive. General description Microsporidia are spore-forming parasites. Although previously classified as proto- zoa, evidence indicates that they could be fungi or closely related to fungi. At least 14 genera and 17 species (out of more than 2000 species) have been implicated in human infections, including Enterocytozoon, Encephalitozoon, Nosema, Pleistophora, Vittaforma and Trachipleistophora, as well as a collective group of unclassified micro- sporidia. Of these, some are zoonotic and others appear to be human specific. There are two main clades of microsporidia: typical (or advanced) and atypical (or primi- tive). Spores of the typical microsporidia are generally 2–8 µm in size, but can vary from 1 µm to greater than 30 µm in length. Within an infected cell, a complex process

324 325 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA of multiplication takes place, and new spores are produced and released in faeces, urine, respiratory secretions or other body fluids. Human health effects Microsporidia cause illness, predominantly in persons with AIDS and others who are immunocompromised, immunosuppressed or immune deficient. The most common symptom in AIDS patients is severe enteritis involving chronic diarrhoea, dehydra- tion, weight loss and wasting. However, a broad range of other illnesses can also occur. Prolonged illness for up to years has been reported. In immunocompetent individu- als, infections can be asymptomatic and where there is illness, symptom are less pro- nounced with the typical illness being gastroenteritis. Epidemiology Microsporidia infections occur worldwide, with documented illness in persons from all continents. The burden of disease with microsporidia is variable and uncertain de- pending on population segment, age, immunocompetence, HIV-infection status and antiretroviral therapy access, geographical region, occupation, extent of contact with animals and sanitation conditions. The microsporidia most frequently found in hu- man infections are Enterocytozoon bieneusi, followed by the Encephalitozoon species, particularly E. intestinalis, followed by E. cuniculi and E. hellem. The overall preva- lence rate of microsporidial infections (based on a 2021 meta-analysis) is estimated to be 10%. Enterocytozoon infection is generally localized and limited to intestinal enterocytes and biliary epithelium. Encephalitozoon spp. can cause systemic infection involving multiple sites, with complications including keratoconjunctivitis, myositis and hepatitis. Several other species are also capable of causing disseminated disease. Transmission Microsporidia can be transmitted by the faecal–oral route through contact with in- fected people, animals or fomites, or ingestion of faecally contaminated water, food or soil. Although spores have been detected in faecally contaminated water and food, waterborne and foodborne outbreaks are rarely reported. Drinking-water is an un- confirmed exposure source. However, microsporidia have been associated with eye infections from exposures to soil, mud and recreational waters. Urine may also be an important source of exposure. Transmission by the inhalation of airborne spores is plausible, but documented evidence is lacking. Epidemiological and experimental studies in mammals suggest that Encephalitozoon spp. can be transmitted horizontally and possibly transplacentally from mother to offspring, but documented evidence is lacking for humans. Although the role of animals in microsporidia transmission to humans remains unclear, zoonotic transmission of some strains is likely. The human infectious dose is unknown. Detection methods Microsporidia can be detected by microscopy, immunoassays or molecular methods. Cell culture and fluorescent in situ hybridization can be used to detect viability (see section 7.4).

326 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Source and occurrence Microsporidia are found in a broad range of water and wastewater environments, and have been detected in surface water, groundwater and drinking-water. Prevalence is influenced by the presence of human and animal wastes including from sewage (un- treated or partially treated). Microsporidia spores can persist for long periods in water (over 1 month at 20 °C). Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4 ), control measures to reduce potential microbial risks should be effective against microsporidia. These include protection of source water from contamination by human and animal wastes, application of adequate water treat- ment processes, and protection of drinking-water quality during storage and distribu- tion. Microsporidia are likely removed by conventional filtration methods. They are moderately resistant to chlorine, although typical doses and contact times used for drinking-water treatment should be sufficient to inactivate microsporidia. Microspo- ridia are sensitive to ozone and UV light. Due to the environmental persistence of microsporidia spores and their moderate resistance to chemical disinfectants, E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator of their absence in drinking- water. However, the presence of E. coli is a suitable indicator of the possible presence of microsporidia. Bibliography WHO (2025) Microsporidia. Naegleria fowleri Significance in drinking‑water Naegleria fowleri is not transmitted through the ingestion of drinking-water. However, there is strong evidence for water-based transmission from water entering nasal pas- sages during recreational activities involving drinking-water (e.g. in swimming pools, playing with garden hoses) and through nasal rinsing and ablution. Naegleria can also harbour bacterial pathogens such as Legionella and may play a role in their survival and pathogenicity in drinking-water. General description Naegleria are free-living amoebae commonly found in warm fresh water and soil. The life cycle of Naegleria consists of three stages. The trophozoite (10–35 μm) is the feed- ing and infective stage, while the cyst (7–15 μm) is the environmentally persistent stage. The amoeba-flagellate (10–16 μm) is a temporary motile stage that develops in response to environmental changes. There are more than 30 species of Naegleria , but only one, N. fowleri, has been isolated from human cases of disease. N. fowleri is ther- mophilic and feeds on bacteria in water and soil. Human health effects N. fowleri causes primary amoebic meningoencephalitis. Infection occurs when tro- phozoites in water are forced up the nasal cavity, migrate through the olfactory nerve

326 327 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA and cause extensive damage to the frontal lobes of the brain. Symptoms include head- ache, fever, nausea and vomiting, rapidly progressing to a stiff neck, seizures, altered mental status, hallucinations and coma. The survival rate (including based on a 2021 review) is less than 5%. Epidemiology Although N. fowleri is widespread in fresh water and soil, primary amoebic menin- goencephalitis is infrequent; only a few hundred cases have been reported worldwide, with reporting in all continents except Antarctica. Exposure is associated with age, gender and activities. Disease associated with exposure to contaminated drinking- water used in recreational activities is highest in male children, while disease associ- ated with nasal ablution or irrigation is highest in adult males. Most cases of disease are associated with recreational exposure to warm fresh water and contaminated drinking-water in warm climates. Transmission N. fowleri is transmitted by contaminated water entering the nasal passages. Trans- mission does not occur through consumption of drinking-water, and there is no person-to-person transmission. Cases associated with drinking-water supplies have typically been associated with conditions that favoured the growth of the organism (e.g. hot weather, inadequate treatment and poor management of drinking-water dis- tribution systems) followed by exposures via swimming pools, playing with garden hoses, nasal ablution and irrigating sinuses. The human infective dose is unknown. The median incubation period for primary amoebic meningoencephalitis is 5 days. The development of illness is rapid, progressing through coma to death within a me- dian of 5 days. Detection methods Naegleria can be detected using culture-based methods, with molecular methods available to confirm the presence of N. fowleri (see section 7.4). Source and occurrence N. fowleri is a natural inhabitant of warm fresh water and soil, and is distributed world- wide with habitats including lakes, streams, groundwater, spas, swimming pools, hy- drotherapy pools and hot springs. The amoebae grow in biofilms in drinking-water distribution systems and storage tanks in the absence of disinfectant residuals provid- ed that the water temperature is consistently 25–42 °C. Increased water temperatures (greater than 25 °C) can also increase colonization by N. fowleri. Cysts form under stressful environmental conditions and can persist for long periods in water. Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4 ), control measures to manage potential risks from N. fowleri should include application of adequate water treatment processes, protec- tion of drinking-water quality during storage and distribution, and minimizing their growth in biofilms in distribution systems and building water systems. Filtration sys- tems designed to remove other protozoa, such as Cryptosporidium are likely to be effective in removing the larger Naegleria cysts and trophozoites. Cysts and tropho-

328 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA zoites are moderately resistant to oxidizing disinfectants such as chlorine, but doses and contact times typically used in drinking-water treatment should provide adequate inactivation. N. fowleri is sensitive to UV light. In distribution systems, maintaining a disinfectant residual provides an effective barrier to N. fowleri. As N. fowleri is a non- faecal, environmental organism that can survive and grow in water, E. coli (or ther - motolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator for its possible presence or absence in drinking-water. Bibliography WHO (2025) Naegleria fowleri. Background document for the WHO Guidelines for drinking- water quality. Geneva, World Health Organization. Toxoplasma gondii Significance in drinking‑water Toxoplasma gondii is a significant zoonotic waterborne pathogen, with strong evi- dence from a number of outbreaks linking transmission to drinking-water. A com- mon risk factor associated with outbreaks is use of unfiltered surface water. General description T. gondii is a coccidian protozoan parasite with a complex life cycle including a sexual component that occurs only in felids and an asexual component that occurs in all warm-blooded animals. Domestic cats and other members of the Felidae family are the definitive host. In the natural life cycle of the parasite, rodents and birds con- taining infective tissue cysts are eaten by felids. Sexual reproduction of the para- site occurs in the intestines of these animals and leads to the formation of oocysts (10–12 µm). Excreted oocysts become infectious in the environment after sporula- tion. Following ingestion, asexual reproduction leads to oocysts transforming into tachyzoites (3–6 µm), which localize in host tissue and transform into bradyzoites that form cysts. In humans, tissue cysts form most commonly in skeletal muscle, myocardium, brain and eyes. Human health effects Toxoplasmosis is usually asymptomatic. In about 10% of cases, symptoms develop and include acute flu-like symptoms and enlargement of the lymph nodes, liver and spleen. The clinical course is usually self-limiting. During chronic infection, dormant tissue cysts persist in the host. In immunocompetent individuals, there is a rare risk of devel- oping ocular toxoplasmosis later in life. In immunodeficient individuals, reactivation of cysts can result in disseminated disease involving the central nervous system and lungs, and lead to severe neurological disorders or pneumonia that can be fatal. If a woman is infected for the first time during pregnancy, the parasite is transmitted to the unborn child in about one third of cases. Infection during the first trimester can lead to severe outcomes including spontaneous abortion, stillbirth or fetal abnormal- ity. Congenital toxoplasmosis from first trimester infections can result in chorioretini- tis, cerebral calcifications, hydrocephalus, severe thrombocytopenia and convulsions. Infections later in pregnancy can be asymptomatic at birth, but ocular toxoplasmosis can occur years later.

328 329 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Epidemiology T. gondii is found throughout the world, but infection is more common in warm and humid climates. The prevalence of human T. gondii infection varies among countries and regions within the same country, with rates (including based on a 2019 systematic review), up to 90% reported. Poor socioeconomic status and the ingestion of raw or undercooked meat increase the risk of infection. The estimated seroprevalence of T. gondii infection in pregnant women varies widely in different parts of the world. Case-control studies in Europe have shown that consuming meat is the main risk fac- tor for infection in pregnant women. In Ethiopia, anti-T. gondii seropositivity among pregnant women was associated with having an unsafe water source as well as age, abortion history, contact with cats, cat ownership, lack of knowledge about toxoplas- mosis and being a housewife. Transmission T. gondii is transmitted via the consumption of raw or undercooked meat contain- ing tissue cysts or through ingestion of oocysts in food such as contaminated vegeta- bles and fruit and raw or undercooked shellfish, in untreated or inadequately treated drinking-water or in surface waters during recreational bathing. T. gondii can be trans- mitted from cats and through ingestion of soil. Humans are an intermediate host and do not excrete oocysts. Person-to-person transmission does not occur except through vertical transmission from mother to child, by organ transplantation or through blood transfusion. The dose–response relationship for ingestion of T. gondii oocysts or tissue cysts has not been established in humans. However, based on animal dose–response data, the relative infectivity of T. gondii is expected to be high (infective doses of 1–10 2 organisms). The incubation period for humans varies depending on the T. gondii life stage initiating infection. Reports from human outbreaks suggest incubation periods of 10–23 days after ingestion of infected tissue cysts and 5–20 days after ingesting oocysts from contaminated environmental matrices. Detection methods Methods for T. gondii include microscopy, molecular techniques, loop-mediated iso- thermal amplification and bioassays. Source and occurrence There are limited data on the occurrence of T. gondii, but they have been detected in water and wastewater environments including surface water, groundwater and inad- equately treated drinking-water. Prevalence is influenced by contamination from wild and domestic cats. Oocysts of T. gondii can persist in water for long periods (over 1 month at 20 °C). Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4 ), control measures to manage potential risks from T. gondii oocysts should include prevention of source water contamination by wild and domestic cats, application of adequate water treatment processes, and protection of drinking-water quality during storage and distribution. Since T. gondii oocysts are

330 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA larger than Cryptosporidium oocysts, filtration processes are important barriers for T. gondii in drinking-water treatment. T. gondii oocysts are highly resistant to chlorine, but are sensitive to UV light. Due to the environmental persistence of T. gondii oocysts and their resistance to chemical disinfectants, the absence of E. coli (or thermotoler - ant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator for their absence in drinking-water. However, the presence of E. coli is a suitable indicator of the possible presence of T. gondii (see section 11.6). Bibliography WHO (2025) Toxoplasma gondii. Geneva, World Health Organization. 11.4 Helminth pathogens The word “helminth” comes from the Greek word meaning “worm” , and refers to all types of worms – free living and parasitic. The major parasitic worms are classified primarily in the phylum Nematoda (roundworms including Dracunculus ) and the phylum Platyhelminthes (flatworms including Fasciola and Schistosoma ). For most helminths, drinking-water is not a significant route of transmission. There are two exceptions: Dracunculus medinensis (guinea worm) and Fasciola (F. hepatica and F. gigantica) (liver flukes). However, for both these exceptions, transmission has been linked to consumption of surface water rather than drinking-water supplies. Dracun- culus and Fasciola both require intermediate hosts to complete their life cycles but are transmitted through drinking-water by different mechanisms. Other helminthiases can be transmitted through water contact (schistosomiasis) or are associated with the use of untreated wastewater in agriculture (ascariasis, trichuriasis, hookworm infec- tions and strongyloidiasis), but are not usually transmitted through drinking-water (for further information, see the background documents for these pathogens prepared for the WHO Guidelines on sanitation and health (WHO, 2025)). Although other free- living nematodes aside from D. medinensis do not cause disease, there is a potential for them to harbour pathogens and provide protection from disinfection. Dracunculus Significance in drinking‑water There is strong evidence for waterborne transmission of Dracunculus medinensis. While the geographical spread of dracunculiasis has been reduced, in the limited number of countries where D. medinensis still occurs, ingestion of surface water con- taminated with infected copepods remains the primary source of infection. Formal drinking-water supplies have not been linked to the transmission of D. medinensis. General description D. medinensis, also called guinea worm, is a nematode (roundworm) that infects peo- ple, dogs and possibly other mammalian hosts. The worm has a complex life cycle involving human (or dog) hosts, copepods (e.g. water fleas, usually cyclops), fish and frogs. Fertilized female worms measure 60–100 cm in length.

330 331 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Human health effects Dracunculiasis (guinea worm disease) becomes apparent about 1 year post ingestion of D. medinensis larvae. The infecting female worm emerges from the skin, typically in the lower leg to produce a painful, debilitating wound that persists until the entire worm exits the body, which is a process that can take many weeks. Slight fever, itchy rash, nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and dizziness may be associated with emergence. Over time, cellulitis, abscesses, sepsis and septic arthritis near the exit wound can oc- cur, causing the joints to lock and deform; secondary tetanus infection can also occur. The wound at the site of worm emergence must be managed hygienically to minimize the risks of secondary bacterial infection. Mortality rates are very low, but permanent disability can result from contractures of tendons. Epidemiology A global eradication campaign that began in the 1980s was responsible for the mass reduction in the number of cases of dracunculiasis and continues to eliminate the pathogen in a few remaining endemic countries in Africa. People of all ages are sus- ceptible to infection and illness. Particular risk groups are the poorest of rural dwellers in low-income settings who use contaminated surface water as a source of drinking- water, often with little or no treatment. A complication in the prevention and control of dracunculiasis is the presence of the same worm in domestic dogs in these under - served settings. Transmission Humans typically become infected with D. medinensis by drinking surface water con- taining copepods harbouring D. medinensis larvae. Humans may also become infected by eating raw or undercooked fish or frogs harbouring copepods. Larvae ingested by humans penetrate the stomach and intestinal wall, mature and migrate throughout the body. The emergence of the fertilized female worm from the skin causes severe pain that often leads infected people to immerse the emerging worm wound in water, resulting in the release of thousands of larvae. These larvae can live for a few days in water. Copepods present in stagnant surface water accumulate immature larvae and support the development of mature, infectious larvae in about 2 weeks. Person-to- person transmission has not been reported. There is no immunity to D. medinensis infection, and reinfection is possible. The human infectious dose of D. medinensis is unknown. Detection methods Analytical methods for D. medinensis in water are difficult. The copepods infected with D. medinensis larvae need to be recovered, and there is no culture system for the worm, except for experimental animals. Detection is currently limited to microscopy, although molecular methods to detect D. medinensis larvae in copepods are being developed (see section 7.4). Source and occurrence D. medinensis is found typically in stagnant surface waters that contain its copepod hosts. Such waters are the natural aquatic reservoirs and human exposure sources for

332 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA this pathogen. In such waters, the copepods containing D. medinensis can persist for long time periods and are endemically present. Hence, the persistence of D. medi - nensis is long (over 1 month at 20 °C). Other Dracunculus species that do not infect humans may also be present in water, further complicating analytical efforts. Accord- ingly, there are no data on occurrence of D. medinensis in water. Prevention and management The provision of a safe water supply to communities relying on surface water sources is a key component to eradicating dracunculiasis. Within a WSP (see chapter 4), con- trol measures that can be applied to prevent transmission of Dracunculus require a comprehensive approach. These include encouraging infected people to avoid enter - ing surface water sources, eradicating copepods from surface water sources with an approved larvicide, preventing entry of infected dogs into water bodies and filtration to remove copepods. Copepods harbouring D. medinensis larvae are sensitive to disin- fectants such as chlorine. This may result in the release of larvae that have low to mod- erate resistance to chlorine, although filtration is the recommended treatment barrier. Since Dracunculus are non-faecal organisms and due to their complex life cycle and environmental survival, E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable in- dicator for their possible presence or absence in drinking-water. Bibliography WHO (2025) Dracunculus. Background document for the WHO Guidelines for drinking-water quality. Geneva, World Health Organization. Fasciola Significance in drinking‑water There is moderate evidence for waterborne transmission of Fasciola from surface water used as sources of drinking-water in hyperendemic areas. General description Fasciola hepatica (known as the common liver fluke) and F. gigantica (known as the giant liver fluke) are trematodes of the family Fasciolidae. Fasciola are vector-borne zoonotic organisms with complex life cycles involving flukes, eggs, miracidia, cer - cariae and infective metacercariae. Development involves passage through human or animal hosts and an intermediate freshwater snail vector. Their natural hosts are mainly mid- and large-sized ruminants and equines. Pigs can be important reservoirs in human endemic areas. Humans can also be an important source of infectious Fas- ciola. Adult F. hepatica and F. gigantica flukes can reach 29 mm and 52 mm in size, respectively, while metacercariae are about 0.2 mm in diameter. Human health effects Infection with Fasciola in humans can cause severe symptoms with acute and chronic stages or can be asymptomatic. The acute stage lasts from 3 to 4 months after inges- tion of metacercariae, and is mainly related to the destruction of the abdominal peri- toneum and liver tissue as the flukes migrate from the intestines to the liver and bile

332 333 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA ducts. Major symptoms include fever, abdominal pain, gastrointestinal disturbances, urticaria and respiratory symptoms. The chronic stage may last from 9 to 13 years after ingestion, and involves inflammation or blockage of the bile ducts or the gall bladder. Clinical manifestations include epigastric pain, fatty food intolerance, nausea, jaun- dice, pruritus, right upper-quadrant abdominal tenderness and biliary colic. Further, more severe, life-threatening complications may also manifest, including anaemia, cir- rhosis and extrahepatic venous thrombosis. Juvenile flukes sometimes deviate during migration and may enter other organs and cause ectopic fascioliasis, which may be highly pathogenic or even fatal when affecting the central nervous system or eye. Epidemiology Estimates of global Fasciola infections (based on a 2020 review) range from 2.4 mil- lion to 17 million people or higher. Human infection varies largely in relation to the distribution of snail vector populations in freshwater bodies and general physio- graphic and climatic conditions, including seasonal patterns influenced by tempera- ture and rainfall. Geographically, F. hepatica is distributed throughout Europe, north- ern and eastern Africa, Asia, Oceania, and the Americas (generally colder countries and higher altitudes). However, F. gigantica is restricted to Africa and southern Asia (generally warmer countries and lowlands). Other factors influencing fascioliasis are climate change, water resource development projects and movement of host animals. In endemic areas, prevalence and intensity of infection peaks in 9–11 year- olds, but infection persists in adults, with females appearing to be more affected. In high-income countries, the peak appears in 30–40 year-olds. However, infection is uncommon in North America, where most cases are associated with travellers and immigrants. Endemic areas are known to occur in several countries in the Ameri- cas, Africa, Asia and the Middle East, with the highest prevalence detected in South America and Africa. Transmission Consumption of infective metacercariae attached to uncooked freshwater plants (e.g. watercress) is the most common route of transmission. Fresh water becomes contami- nated when eggs are excreted by infected human and animal hosts, miracidia hatch from the eggs and penetrate an intermediate snail host where cercariae are developed (larvae), which are released into water. Cercariae swim for a short period until they reach a suitable attachment site (aquatic plants), where they encyst to form meta- cercariae, which become infective within 24 hours. In addition to consumption of aquatic plants, drinking-water contaminated with metacercariae and consumption of contaminated beverages, juices and soups are receiving increasing attention as sources of fascioliasis. Washing of vegetables, fruits and kitchen utensils with contaminated water can also be sources of disease. The high diversity of infection sources and their heterogeneity in different countries underlie the large epidemiological heterogene- ity of human fascioliasis. Person-to-person transmission is not possible due to the complex life cycle. Evidence indicates that metacercariae are highly infective (infective doses of 1–102 organisms), but the infective dose has not been determined.

334 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Detection methods Metacercariae in water may be identified by microscopic observation following filtra- tion. Molecular methods are useful to confirm the classification of metacercariae as Fasciola (see section 7.4). Source and occurrence Fasciola occur in different types of fresh water, linked to excretion of eggs from in- fected human and animal hosts and the distribution of the snail vector populations. Lymnaeids prefer stagnant water, and their high colonization capacity explains their presence in waterbodies including springs, artificial fountains and dams. Temporary water bodies inhabited by lymnaeids explain links between seasonal transmission and rainy seasons, such as the monsoon period in south central Asia. Permanent water bodies inhabited by lymnaeids in high-altitude and high-evapotranspiration areas where monthly temperature variations are small allow for disease transmission throughout the year. Fasciola are not found in groundwater since lymnaeids need light to survive. Reports on the prevalence of Fasciola in drinking-water are limited. Metacercariae have a hard outer wall and can survive for long periods in water (over 1 month at 20 °C), but are susceptible to high temperatures and sunlight. Prevention and management Within a WSP (see chapter 4 ), control measures to manage potential risks from Fasciola should include protection of source waters from human and animal faeces, application of adequate water treatment processes, and protection of storage and dis- tribution systems from external contamination. Based on morphology and resistance to environmental pressures, metacercariae are likely to be relatively resistant to disin- fection. However, based on their size, they should be removed by physical processes. Due to the complex life cycle and environmental survival of Fasciola , E. coli (or ther- motolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator for their possible presence or absence in drinking-water. Bibliography WHO (2025) Fasciola. Background document for the WHO Guidelines for drinking-water quality and the WHO Guidelines on sanitation and health. Geneva, World Health Organization. Free-living nematodes Significance in drinking‑water Free-living nematodes (excluding Dracunculus medinensis, which is the subject of a separate fact sheet) do not cause disease. Potential risks have been identified due to free-living nematodes harbouring pathogens and providing protection from disinfec- tion. However, there have been no outbreaks of waterborne diseases caused by patho- gens carried by free-living nematodes. In poorly maintained drinking-water systems, free-living nematodes may survive and grow in biofilms, but there is little evidence that they cause a deterioration in the aesthetic quality of drinking-water.

334 335 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA General description Nematoda (roundworms) are a diverse animal phylum; they are structurally simple, with the digestive tract running from the mouth to the opening near the tail. The ma- jority of species are not parasitic and are described as free living, i.e. they live entirely in the natural environment (water and soil). Food sources for different nematodes include algae, fungi, protozoa, dead matter and meiofauna. At optimal temperatures, free-living nematodes range in size from 0.5 to 1.6 mm. A limited number of nem- atodes have a complete or partial parasitic life cycle and are pathogenic. Only one (D. medinensis) is a human pathogen and can be transmitted through drinking-water; it is the subject of a separate fact sheet. Human health effects Free-living nematodes are not infectious and do not present a direct threat to human health. However, they may harbour pathogenic microorganisms and potentially pro- tect them from disinfection processes used in drinking-water treatment. For example, studies have indicated their potential to be transport hosts of enteric pathogenic bac- teria and protozoa. Gram-negative bacteria ingested by free-living nematodes have been shown to survive the presence of chlorine and UV light. Epidemiology Since free-living nematodes are not responsible for infectious diseases in humans, this section is not applicable. Transmission Although humans can be exposed to free-living nematodes through ingestion of water and consumption of fresh vegetables, there is no indication that they cause infections. Detection methods Free-living nematodes may be identified by microscopic examination of particulate matter concentrated by filtration of water. Distinguishing pathogenic larvae of hook- worm and threadworm from free-living, non-pathogenic nematodes in water is dif- ficult and requires special knowledge of nematology. Source and occurrence Free-living nematodes are ubiquitous in soil and water environments, and have been detected in drinking-water supplies. They may enter the drinking-water supply chain at any stage, although investigations on occurrence in drinking-water have been lim- ited. Higher numbers have been found at higher water temperatures and when turbid- ity and nutrient levels of source waters are high. Prevention and management Although free-living nematodes are of low concern in drinking-water supplies, con- trol measures within a WSP (see chapter 4 ) to protect source waters from the input of nutrients, ensure adequate water treatment processes, and protect drinking-water quality during storage and distribution will reduce the presence of free-living nema- todes. There is little quantitative information on the removal and/or inactivation of

336 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA free-living nematodes by drinking-water treatment processes. However, based on their size, they should be removed by filtration, but some may colonize granular and bio- logical filters and may subsequently be released into drinking-water. Regular back- washing and maintenance of filters should reduce the accumulation of nematodes. Free-living nematodes are highly resistant to chlorine and UV light, and will not be inactivated by doses typically used to disinfect drinking-water. Maintenance proce- dures to safeguard the cleanliness of distribution systems, such as scheduled flushing of pipes, should reduce the presence of free-living nematodes in distribution systems. As free-living nematodes are non-faecal environmental organisms, E. coli (or thermo- tolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator for their possible presence or absence in drinking-water. Bibliography WHO (2025) Free-living nematodes. Background document for the WHO Guidelines for drinking- water quality. Geneva, World Health Organization. Schistosoma Significance in drinking‑water There is no evidence linking transmission of schistosomiasis with ingestion of con- taminated drinking-water. However, there is strong evidence linking transmission to poor sanitation and lack of safe drinking-water. Readily available safe drinking-water contributes to disease prevention by reducing use of infested water for domestic pur- poses (e.g. washing clothes, bathing). General description Schistosoma (commonly known as blood flukes) is a genus of trematodes. There are 23 species of Schistosoma . Most human infections are caused by S. haematobium , S. mansoni and S. japonicum, but other species can infect humans, namely S. mekongi, S. guineensis and S. intercalatum. Humans are the definitive hosts of human schis- tosomes, but animal species have been reported to be infected with human schis- tosomes. Schistosoma have a complex life cycle involving flukes, eggs and infective cercaria and involves passage through an intermediate snail vector and a definitive vertebrate host, which may be human and/or animal, depending on the species. Schistosoma flukes can be 7–20 mm long and infective cercariae 0.4–0.6 µm long. Schistosoma flukes can live and produce eggs in their human hosts for several years, with initial egg production taking 3–4 months after exposure. Human health effects Infection with Schistosoma can lead to two main forms of disease. Symptoms of schis- tosomiasis typically result from the immune response to eggs in tissues, and not from the flukes themselves. Therefore, the symptoms depend on the amount and location of eggs in the body. Urogenital schistosomiasis (caused by S. haematobium ) typically manifests as presence of blood in urine. Long-term urogenital schistosomiasis can cause bladder cancer and renal failure. Urogenital schistosomiasis can also cause geni- tal lesions in men and women. In women, potential complications include miscarriag-

336 337 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA es, ectopic pregnancy and infertility. Intestinal schistosomiasis (caused by S. mansoni, S. japonicum, S. intercalatum, S. guineensis and S. mekongi) produces abdominal pains, diarrhoea, blood in stools, and enlargement of the liver and spleen. Life-threatening complications arising from chronic infections include liver fibrosis and portal hyper- tension. Anaemia and malnutrition can be associated with the disease, with potential long-term effects on growth and cognitive development in children. In some people, acute schistosomiasis (Katayama fever), including fever, rash, chills, enlarged liver and spleen, muscle pain and cough, can begin within 1–2 months post infection, particu- larly with S. japonicum. If cercariae of avian schistosomes penetrate the human skin, they can cause an inflammatory response at the point of penetration known as schisto- some cercarial dermatitis (or more commonly swimmer’s itch). Epidemiology It has been estimated (including as reported in a 2023 WHO fact sheet) that schis- tosomiasis affects over 250 million people worldwide. Global distribution of schisto- somiasis varies by causative species, since each has a specific range of suitable snail hosts. For example, S. haematobium and S. mansoni are found in Africa, while the lat- ter is also found in the Middle East, Caribbean and South America and S. japonicum is found in China, Indonesia and the Philippines. Most infections occur in poor communities with lack of access to safe drinking- water and inadequate sanitation. In endemic areas, incidence varies spatially and sea- sonally with distance to water bodies, rainfall, temperature and irrigation practices that influence exposure and the snail host. Prevalence of infection is linked to the proportion of a population having contact with contaminated surface water, as well as frequency and duration of contact. Exposure occurs through domestic, occupa- tional or recreational activities involving water contact. Use of untreated faecal sludge and wastewater in agriculture has been associated with increased risk of schistosome infections. People of all ages are susceptible to infection, but school-age children are particularly vulnerable due to increased swimming and fishing in contaminated water and inadequate hygiene. Transmission Transmission of Schistosoma is caused primarily by contact with water contaminated with cercariae, which can penetrate skin. Infection does not occur through ingestion of drinking-water. Fresh water becomes contaminated by Schistosoma eggs when in- fected people (or animals) defecate or urinate in the water. The eggs hatch, invade intermediate snail hosts and develop into infective cercariae (larvae), which are re- leased into water after several weeks. Once released from the host snail, cercariae can remain infective to humans for 1–3 days in fresh water. Shedding of eggs can be years, if not decades. There is some evidence of increasing age-associated immunity in endemic populations. Detection methods Schistosome eggs in faeces and urine are detected via microscopic examination and molecular methods (see section 7.4). Qualitative methods for the detection of cer - cariae in standing water are also available.

338 11. MICROBIAL FACT SHEETS GUIDELINES FOR DRINKING-WATER QUALITY: FOURTH EDITION INCORPORATING THE FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD ADDENDA Source and occurrence The distribution of schistosomes is largely dependent on the availability of freshwater habitats for the snail host, such as ponds, lakes and slow-flowing streams. Water re- source development projects have been identified as potential sources of elevated and shifting rates of schistosomiasis as a result of the creation of new habitats for fresh- water snails. In endemic areas, surface waters containing host snails are susceptible to contamination by schistosome eggs in faeces and urine. Schistosome eggs can survive days to weeks outside water, but require contact with freshwater and snail vectors to complete their life cycle. Eggs deposited near water bodies through open defecation and urination may still hatch if washed into the water bodies by rain. There is limited data on the occurrence of schistosome eggs and cercariae in surface water. Schisto- some eggs cannot survive and complete their life cycle in groundwater; similarly, it is unlikely that cercariae could contaminate groundwater. Prevention and management Providing safe drinking-water is a key pillar for controlling schistosomiasis. Within a WSP (see chapter 4 ), control measures to manage potential risks from Schistosoma should include protection of source waters from human and animal faeces and urine, snail control programmes, application of adequate water treatment processes, and pro- tection of storage and distribution systems from external contamination. Schistosome cercariae can be removed from water by filtration. Although schistosome cercariae are moderately resistant to chlorine, doses and contact times typically used in drinking- water treatment are effective for inactivating cercariae. UV light is also an effective dis- infectant for schistosome cercariae. Due to the complex life cycle and environmental survival of Schistosoma, E. coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) is not a suitable indicator for the possible presence or absence of Schistosoma in drinking-water.
